verse.text: In my first account, Theophilus, I wrote about everything that Jesus began to do and to teach

note.traditional: the former treatise; the first book

verse.note: The reference is to the Gospel of Luke, which is addressed to the same Theophilus and which Acts continues. The Greek word was a normal term for one volume of a longer work.

verse.text: until the day he was taken up, after he had given instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen.
To them he also presented himself alive after his suffering by many convincing proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.
And while eating with them, he ordered them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Father, “which you heard from me;

note.traditional: being assembled together with them; while staying with them

verse.note: The Greek verb is rare and its sense here is disputed. It may mean “eating with,” “gathering together with,” or, as a spelling variant of a similar verb, “staying with.” “Eating with” has ancient support and fits Luke’s emphasis elsewhere that the risen Jesus ate with his disciples (Luke 24:41–43; Acts 10:41), but many translations choose one of the other options.

text.q: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

verse.text: So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you restoring the kingdom to Israel at this time?”
He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has set by his own authority,

text.q: but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth.”

verse.text: After he said this, as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.
And as they were gazing into heaven while he was going, suddenly two men in white clothes were standing beside them.
verse.note: This is how Luke describes angels: the “two men in dazzling clothes” at the tomb in Luke 24:4 are called angels in Luke 24:23, and Acts 10 describes the same figure both as an angel and as a man in bright clothing. Their words here are therefore marked as angelic speech, though the text itself says only “men.”

verse.text: They said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from what is called the Mount of Olives, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.
verse.note: This was the distance Jewish tradition allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath without breaking the rest, reckoned at two thousand cubits, a little over half a mile or about one kilometer. Luke uses it simply as a measure of distance.

verse.text: When they had entered the city, they went up to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James.
verse.note: The word means someone zealous or fervently devoted, often for God’s law. Whether it marks Simon as a member of a revolutionary movement is uncertain, since an organized party called the Zealots is clearly attested only some decades later, around the war with Rome. The epithet may simply describe his religious fervor.

The Greek says only “Judas of James.” This construction normally names a father, as it does for “James of Alphaeus” in the same list, and most modern translations render it “son of James.” The King James Version took it as “brother,” identifying him with the Jude of Jude 1.

verse.text: All these were devoting themselves with one mind to prayer, together with some women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.
In those days Peter stood up among the brothers and sisters (the crowd of people gathered together was about one hundred twenty) and said,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to refer to a mixed group of siblings or fellow members of a community, and the group here includes the women of verse 14. Many translations keep “brothers,” and some use “believers.” In verse 16 Peter’s address adds the word for “men,” a formal way of opening a speech, and is rendered “Brothers.”

text.q: “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David about Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus,
for he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this service.”

verse.note: Most translations have “ministry” here. In the first century the word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession, so “service,” a standard lexicon gloss, is used throughout this translation.

verse.text: (Now this man acquired a field with the wages of his wrongdoing, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out.

note.term: Now this man acquired a field

verse.note: Verses 18 and 19 are set off here as an aside by the narrator, not as part of Peter’s speech. This is the view of most modern editors and translations. Peter would hardly need to tell residents of Jerusalem what was known to all Jerusalem or to translate a word from “their own language.” Some translations nevertheless leave the verses within the speech.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a worker’s pay, and here it refers to the money Judas was paid for betraying Jesus. English translations vary among “reward,” “wages” and “payment.” “Wages” is used in this translation wherever the phrase “wages of wrongdoing” occurs.

The Greek phrase normally means “becoming prone,” that is, falling face down. A minority of scholars, following some ancient interpreters, take it as “swelling up.” Matthew 27:3–10 gives a different account, in which Judas hangs himself and the priests buy the field. How the two accounts relate is debated.

verse.text: It became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)

text.q: “For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one living in it,’ and, ‘Let another take his position as overseer.’

note.term: it is written in the book of Psalms

verse.note: The two quotations are from Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8, in the wording of the Greek translation of the Psalms. Both psalms are prayers of a righteous sufferer against his enemies. The first is plural in the psalm (“their”) and is applied here in the singular to Judas.

text.q: So, of the men who accompanied us during the whole time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,
beginning from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.”

verse.text: So they put forward two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also known as Justus, and Matthias.
Then they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen

text.q: to take the place in this service and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.”

verse.text: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles.
When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place.
verse.note: Pentecost (“fiftieth”) is the Greek name for the Jewish Festival of Weeks, a harvest festival held fifty days after Passover. It was one of the pilgrimage festivals, which explains why Jerusalem is full of Jews from many lands in the verses that follow.

verse.text: Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like the rushing of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.
And tongues as of fire appeared to them, dividing among them, and one came to rest on each of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit enabled them to speak out.
verse.note: The Greek word means both the tongue and a language, and Luke plays on it: tongues of fire in verse 3, speech in other tongues here. Verses 6–11 make clear that real foreign languages, understood by their native speakers, are meant. Many modern versions translate “other languages” here, which is accurate but loses the wordplay.

verse.text: Now there were Jews living in Jerusalem, devout men from every nation under heaven.
verse.note: The same Greek word in the plural is elsewhere translated “Gentiles,” meaning the non-Jewish peoples. Here it means peoples as ethnic units. The men in view are Jews who came from all those nations, not non-Jews.

verse.text: At this sound the crowd came together and was thrown into confusion, because each one heard them speaking in his own language.
They were astounded and marveled, saying, “Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans?

text.q: So how is it that we hear, each of us, in our own language, the one we were born into?
Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those living in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia,
Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own tongues of the great deeds of God.”

verse.text: All were astounded and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?”
But others mocked and said, “They are full of sweet wine.”
But Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke out to them: “Fellow Jews and all you who live in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words.

text.q: These people are not drunk, as you suppose, for it is only the third hour of the day.

note.term: the third hour of the day
note.traditional: the third hour of the day

verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning. Peter’s point is that it is far too early in the day for anyone to be drunk.

text.q: No, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel:

‘And it shall be in the last days, God says, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy, and your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.
Even on my slaves, both men and women, in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy.

note.term: my slaves, both men and women
note.traditional: my servants and my handmaidens; my male servants and female servants

verse.note: The Greek words are the ordinary ones for male and female slaves, people owned by a master, and not for hired servants. In Joel the point is that the Spirit reaches even the lowest social rank; the added “my” makes them God’s own slaves. Many translations soften this to “servants,” though some modern versions have “slaves.”

text.q: And I will give wonders in the sky above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and a mist of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes.
And it shall be that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’
Fellow Israelites, hear these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man attested to you by God with deeds of power and wonders and signs that God did through him among you, as you yourselves know—

verse.note: The Greek is simply the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural of acts that display it. “Deeds of power” keeps that connection visible and keeps the word distinct from “wonders” and “signs” beside it. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is an acceptable rendering.

text.q: this man, handed over by the fixed plan and foreknowledge of God, you nailed up by the hands of lawless men and killed.

verse.note: The word can mean “wicked” in general or “without the Law,” a Jewish way of referring to Gentiles. Many scholars think the second is meant here, pointing to the Romans who carried out the crucifixion. The rendering keeps the traditional phrase, which allows either sense.

text.q: But God raised him up, having loosed the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.

note.traditional: the pains of death; the pangs of death

verse.note: The word normally means labor pains. The phrase comes from the Greek version of the Psalms (Psalm 18:4; 116:3), where the underlying Hebrew is usually understood as “cords of death,” which suits the verb “loosed.” Some interpreters think Luke intends the image of death in labor, unable to hold back what it must deliver.

text.q: For David says of him: ‘I saw the Lord before me always, for he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken.
Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced; and more, my flesh also will dwell in hope,
because you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your Holy One see decay.
You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with gladness in your presence.’
Brothers, I may speak to you plainly about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this day.

verse.note: The word means frank, unreserved speech. Here Peter is stating an obvious fact without hedging—David is dead and his tomb is there to see—so “plainly” fits better than “boldly.” Translations vary between “freely,” “confidently” and “frankly”; the difference is one of English nuance.

text.q: So, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath to seat one from the fruit of his loins on his throne,
he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of the Messiah: that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see decay.

verse.note: The Greek word means “anointed one” and here is a title for the king Israel expected, not a name. “Messiah” is used where the title is the point, as here and in verse 36; “Christ” is kept where it is joined to “Jesus” as in verse 38. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: This Jesus God raised up, and of that we are all witnesses.
Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you see and hear.

note.term: to the right hand of God
note.traditional: by the right hand of God; at the right hand of God

verse.note: The Greek can mean either “to” (or “at”) God’s right hand, the place of honor, or “by” God’s right hand, the instrument of his power. The first fits the quotation that follows (“Sit at my right hand”) and is the choice of most modern versions; the second has the support of the KJV and a number of scholars.

text.q: For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’
Therefore let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Messiah—this Jesus whom you crucified.”

verse.text: When they heard this, they were pierced to the heart and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?”
Peter said to them, “Turn back, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: “Repent” now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord our God calls to himself.”

verse.text: With many other words he bore solemn witness and kept urging them, saying, “Be saved from this crooked generation.”
verse.note: The Greek verb is passive, “be saved,” matching the passive in verse 47 (“those who were being saved”) and Joel’s “will be saved” in verse 21. Many translations have “Save yourselves,” taking the passive in a reflexive sense, which is grammatically possible.

verse.text: So those who accepted his word were baptized, and about three thousand people were added that day.
They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.
verse.note: The word means having something in common and is stronger than modern “fellowship” may suggest. Interpreters are divided over whether it refers here to the community’s shared life in general or specifically to the sharing of goods described in verses 44–45.

verse.text: Awe came upon everyone, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles.
All who believed were together and had everything in common,
and they would sell their property and possessions and distribute the proceeds to all, as anyone had need.
Day by day, as they devoted themselves with one accord to meeting in the temple and broke bread from house to house, they shared their food with joy and simplicity of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. And day by day the Lord added to their number those who were being saved.
Now Peter and John were going up to the temple for the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth hour is about three in the afternoon. This was the time of the afternoon sacrifice in the temple and a customary time of prayer.

verse.text: And a man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried in, whom they set down every day at the temple gate called Beautiful to ask for alms from those going into the temple.
verse.note: No other ancient source uses this name for a temple gate. It is often identified with a great bronze gate on the east side of the temple courts, but the identification is uncertain.

verse.text: When he saw Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.”
He fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
But Peter said, “Silver and gold I do not have, but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk!”
verse.note: Many manuscripts read “rise up and walk.” The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading found in some of the earliest witnesses, on the view that the longer form was filled out from similar healing stories in the Gospels.

verse.text: And grasping him by the right hand, he raised him up. Immediately his feet and ankles were made strong,
and leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and he went into the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
And all the people saw him walking and praising God,
and they recognized him as the one who used to sit asking for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
While he clung to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them at the colonnade called Solomon’s, struck with wonder.
When Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why are you marveling at this, or why do you look so intently at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?

text.q: The God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus, whom you handed over and denied before Pilate, though he had decided to release him.

note.traditional: his Son Jesus (KJV); his servant Jesus (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek word can mean either “child” or “servant.” Most scholars hold that “servant” is meant here, because “has glorified his servant” echoes the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where the Lord’s servant is “glorified,” and because the same word is used of David as God’s servant in Acts 4:25. The same word recurs in verse 26.

text.q: But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you,
and you killed the author of life, whom God raised from the dead; of this we are witnesses.

note.traditional: Prince of life (KJV); Author of life (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek word was used for a leader, a founder, or the originator of something. It can mean here either the one who is the source of life or the one who leads the way into life, and the Greek does not decide between them. “Author” is used in the sense of originator, in pointed contrast with “you killed.”

text.q: And on the basis of faith in his name, his name has made strong this man whom you see and know; the faith that comes through him has given him this complete health in front of all of you.

verse.note: The Greek of this verse is awkward and literally reads “on the faith of his name.” Most interpreters take it as faith in the name of Jesus, but the text does not say whether the faith is that of the apostles, of the healed man, or both. “The faith that comes through him” most likely means faith that Jesus himself makes possible.

text.q: And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers also.
But what God announced beforehand through the mouth of all the prophets, that his Messiah would suffer, he has fulfilled in this way.

verse.note: The Greek word means “anointed one” and here is a title for the king Israel expected, not a name. “Messiah” is used where the title is the point, as here and in verse 20, and “Christ” where the word is attached to “Jesus” as a name, as in verse 6. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: Turn back, then, and return, that your sins may be wiped out,

verse.note: “Repent” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life. The verb that follows it, “return,” is a different Greek word with a closely related meaning.

text.q: so that seasons of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Messiah appointed for you, Jesus,
whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things, of which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old.

note.term: the restoration of all things, of which God spoke

verse.note: The Greek can also be read as “the establishment of all that God spoke,” meaning the time when everything the prophets foretold comes to pass. The noun more usually means restoration to an earlier or proper state, and the related verb is used in Acts 1:6 of restoring the kingdom to Israel, so most translations render it as here.

text.q: Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You shall listen to him in everything he says to you.

verse.note: Manuscripts vary here between “the Lord God,” “the Lord your God,” and “the Lord our God.” The SBLGNT prints the shortest form; the others are probably adjustments toward the wording of Deuteronomy.

text.q: And it will be that every person who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’

note.term: will be utterly destroyed from among the people

verse.note: Peter’s quotation in verses 22–23 draws on Deuteronomy 18:15–19, where Moses promises a prophet like himself. The warning here is worded in the language of Leviticus 23:29, which speaks of a person being cut off from the people. Combining related passages in this way was a common practice in Jewish citation of Scripture.

text.q: And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also announced these days.
You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’
It was for you first that God raised up his servant and sent him to bless you by turning each of you away from your wicked ways.”

verse.note: The verb is the same one used in verse 22 for God “raising up” a prophet, and most interpreters take it here in that sense: God brought Jesus onto the scene and sent him to Israel. It is also a regular word for raising from the dead, and some understand it of the resurrection. The rendering keeps the link with verse 22 and leaves both readings open.

verse.text: While they were speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple, and the Sadducees came upon them,
greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead,
verse.note: The Sadducees, the party of the priestly aristocracy, denied that the dead would be raised (Acts 23:8). The apostles were proclaiming that in the case of Jesus the resurrection had already happened, which challenged both the Sadducees’ teaching and their authority in the temple.

verse.text: and they seized them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening.
But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
The next day their rulers, elders, and scribes gathered in Jerusalem,
along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family,
verse.note: Annas had been deposed from the high priesthood by the Romans about fifteen years earlier; the officiating high priest at this time was his son-in-law Caiaphas. Luke gives Annas the title all the same (as in Luke 3:2), probably because he remained the head of the dominant high-priestly family. John and Alexander are otherwise unknown.

verse.text: and they stood them in the middle and began to ask, “By what power or by what name did you do this?”
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders,

text.q: if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a disabled man, by what means this man has been made well,

verse.note: The Greek verb means both “heal” and “save,” and the same verb and its noun return in verse 12 as “saved” and “salvation.” Peter’s argument moves on that double sense: the name that restored this man’s body is the only one that rescues anyone. English needs two different words.

text.q: let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man stands before you healthy.
He is the stone scorned by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.

verse.note: Peter alludes to Psalm 118:22, but the verb here is not the one the Greek Psalm uses for “rejected.” It means to treat as worthless or with contempt, and the translation keeps that sharper sense. Most versions use “rejected” to match the familiar wording of the Psalm.

The Greek is literally “head of the corner.” It may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes it; scholars are divided. In either case it is the stone on which the structure depends.

text.q: And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved.”

verse.text: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John and grasped that they were unschooled and untrained men, they were amazed, and they recognized that they had been with Jesus.
verse.note: The first word can mean “illiterate” but here more probably means that they lacked formal training in the Law such as the scribes had. The second describes a layperson or non-expert and carries no suggestion of stupidity. The council’s surprise is that men without credentials argue so boldly.

verse.text: And seeing the man who had been cured standing with them, they had nothing to say in reply.
So they ordered them to go outside the council and conferred with one another,
saying, “What are we to do with these men? For that a remarkable sign has taken place through them is plain to all who live in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.

text.q: But so that it spreads no further among the people, let us threaten them, so that they no longer speak in this name to anyone at all.”

verse.text: So they called them in and ordered them not to utter a word or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than to God, you be the judges;
verse.note: This is the adjective elsewhere rendered “righteous” or “just.” Here it stands in the impersonal expression “it is right,” for which English does not use “righteous,” so the traditional “right” is kept.

text.q: for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

verse.text: After threatening them further, they released them, finding no way to punish them because of the people, since all were glorifying God for what had happened;
for the man on whom this sign of healing had been performed was more than forty years old.
After their release they went to their own people and reported everything the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
When they heard it, they raised their voice together to God and said, “Master, you are the one who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them,
verse.note: The word is not the usual one for “Lord” (which comes in verse 29) but the term for the master of a household or an absolute ruler. Most modern versions render it “Sovereign Lord” and the King James Version “Lord.” “Master” keeps it distinct and matches the believers’ description of themselves as his “slaves” in verse 29.

text.q: who said by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant: ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot empty things?

note.term: by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant

verse.note: The Greek of the earliest manuscripts is grammatically tangled at this point, and later manuscripts smooth it to “who by the mouth of your servant David said.” Many scholars suspect an early copying error. The translation gives the sense generally agreed on; the quotation is Psalm 2:1–2.

One Greek word means both “nations” and “Gentiles” (the non-Jewish peoples). English versions of the Psalm usually have “nations,” but “Gentiles” is used here because verse 27 applies the same word to the Romans who joined in condemning Jesus.

text.q: The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Messiah.’

verse.note: The Greek word means “anointed one” and in the Psalm refers to the Lord’s anointed king; older versions have “his Christ” and several modern ones “his Anointed.” “Messiah” is used because the title is the point. Verse 27 picks the word up with the related verb in “whom you anointed.”

text.q: For truly in this city they gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed—both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel—

verse.note: The word can mean either “child” or “servant.” The King James Version has “child” here, but the same word is used of David in verse 25, and most scholars see an echo of the “servant of the Lord” in Isaiah, so “servant” is used for both.

text.q: to do whatever your hand and your plan had decided beforehand should happen.
And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant your slaves to speak your word with all boldness,

verse.note: The word is the ordinary Greek term for a slave, someone owned by a master, and differs from the word translated “servant” in verses 25, 27 and 30. Most versions soften it to “servants.” In the Greek Old Testament it is also an honorable self-description for those wholly at God’s disposal.

text.q: while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders take place through the name of your holy servant Jesus.”

verse.text: When they had prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and went on speaking the word of God with boldness.
Now the community of those who had believed was one in heart and soul, and not one of them said that anything he possessed was his own, but they had everything in common.
With great power the apostles kept giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verse.note: The word may mean God’s favor resting on the believers, or the goodwill of the people of Jerusalem toward them, as in Acts 2:47. The following verse, which begins with “for” and describes their generosity, fits either reading.

verse.text: For there was no one in need among them, because all who owned land or houses would sell them and bring the proceeds of what was sold
and lay them at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as anyone had need.
Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas—which translated means “son of encouragement”—a Levite, a Cypriot by birth,
verse.note: The Greek noun covers encouragement, comfort and exhortation, so “son of consolation” and “son of exhortation” are also possible. “Son of” is a Semitic way of describing a person’s character. Which Aramaic or Hebrew words lie behind Luke’s explanation of the name is uncertain.

verse.text: owned a field; he sold it, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property
and kept back for himself some of the proceeds, with his wife also aware of it; and he brought a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to misappropriate or skim off for oneself. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses of Achan, who secretly took devoted plunder at Jericho (Joshua 7:1), and many scholars think the echo is intended. As verse 4 makes clear, the offense was not keeping some of the money, which was his to keep, but pretending to hand over all of it.

verse.text: Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back for yourself some of the proceeds of the land?

text.q: While it remained unsold, did it not remain yours? And once it was sold, was it not under your own authority? How is it that you conceived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to human beings but to God.”

verse.text: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it.
The younger men got up, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.
After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened.
Peter said to her, “Tell me, did you two sell the land for this much?” She said, “Yes, for this much.”
Then Peter said to her, “How is it that you two agreed to put the Spirit of the Lord to the test? Look, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.”

note.term: put the Spirit of the Lord to the test
note.traditional: tempt the Spirit of the Lord

verse.note: The verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel testing God in the wilderness. Older English versions have “tempt,” which now suggests enticing someone to sin; most modern translations use “test” here.

verse.text: At once she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
And great fear came upon the whole assembly and upon all who heard of these things.
verse.note: This is the first use of the word in Acts in the earliest manuscripts. A first-century reader knew it as the term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution, so “assembly” is used throughout this translation.

verse.text: Many signs and wonders were being done among the people through the hands of the apostles. And they were all together, of one mind, in Solomon’s Colonnade.
None of the rest dared to join them, but the people held them in high esteem,

note.traditional: of the rest durst no man join himself to them

verse.note: The Greek does not say who “the rest” are. They may be outsiders who admired the believers but kept a wary distance after the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, or other believers who did not presume to attach themselves to the apostles. The first reading sits in some tension with verse 14, and interpreters remain divided.

verse.text: and more than ever believers in the Lord were added, crowds of both men and women,

note.term: believers in the Lord were added
note.traditional: believers were the more added to the Lord

verse.note: The words “the Lord” can go with either verb: “those believing in the Lord were added” or “believers were added to the Lord.” Both are grammatical, and translations are split between them.

verse.text: so that they even carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, in order that when Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them.
A crowd also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and all of them were healed.
Then the high priest rose up, along with all who were with him—that is, the party of the Sadducees—and they were filled with jealousy
verse.note: The Greek word covers both envy and zeal. Most translations take it as jealousy of the apostles’ popularity. It could also be religious zeal, the indignation of men who believed they were defending God’s honor.

verse.text: and seized the apostles and put them in public custody.
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the prison, led them out, and said,

text.q: “Go, stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this life.”

verse.text: When they heard this, they went into the temple at daybreak and began teaching. Meanwhile the high priest and those with him arrived, called together the council and the whole body of elders of the sons of Israel, and sent to the jail to have them brought.

note.term: the council and the whole body of elders of the sons of Israel
note.traditional: the council and all the senate of the children of Israel

verse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish court in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest. The “and” may be explanatory (“the council, that is, the whole body of elders”), since no second governing body is known. The solemn phrasing echoes Old Testament language for Israel’s elders.

verse.text: But when the officers arrived, they did not find them in the prison. They returned and reported,

text.q: “We found the jail locked up quite securely and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.”

verse.text: When the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were completely at a loss about them, wondering what this might come to.
Then someone arrived and reported to them, “Look! The men you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”
Then the captain went off with the officers and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people.
When they had brought them, they stood them before the council. The high priest questioned them,
saying, “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name, and look—you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you want to bring this man’s blood upon us.”
Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than human beings.

text.q: The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you put to death by hanging him on a tree.

verse.note: The Greek word means wood or anything made of it, and here refers to the cross. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where a man hanged on a tree is under God’s curse. The apostles’ wording therefore sharpens the charge: the council treated as accursed the one whom God then exalted.

text.q: God exalted this man to his right hand as Leader and Savior, to grant Israel turning back and forgiveness of sins.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call for Israel to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turning back” is used for this word group throughout this translation.

text.q: And we are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

verse.text: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them.
But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the Law honored by all the people, stood up in the council and ordered the men to be put outside for a little while.
Then he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men.

text.q: For some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men rallied to him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing.

verse.note: The Jewish historian Josephus describes a Theudas whose movement was crushed under the governor Fadus, around AD 44–46. That is some years after this scene and decades after Judas the Galilean, whose revolt at the census of AD 6 Gamaliel places later. Either the chronology here differs from that of Josephus, or an otherwise unknown earlier Theudas is meant; scholars are divided.

text.q: After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew people away after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered.
So in the present case I tell you: stay away from these men and leave them alone. For if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will be overthrown;

verse.text: but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them. Otherwise you may even be found fighting against God.” They were persuaded by him,
and after calling in the apostles and having them flogged, they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus and released them.
So they went out from the presence of the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the name.
And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and announcing the good news that the Messiah is Jesus.

note.term: the good news that the Messiah is Jesus

verse.note: The Greek has the article with “Christ,” which marks it here as a title rather than part of a name, so “Messiah” is used. The phrase can be read “that the Messiah is Jesus” or “Jesus as the Messiah”; older versions have simply “Jesus Christ.” The verb, traditionally “preach” or “preach the gospel,” is the ordinary word for announcing good news.

verse.text: Now in these days, as the disciples were multiplying, there arose a grumbling of the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily serving.
verse.note: Both groups here are Jewish followers of Jesus in Jerusalem. The usual view is that the “Hellenists” were Jews whose main language was Greek, many of them from the diaspora, while the “Hebrews” spoke Aramaic or Hebrew. The word is rare and its exact scope is debated, but the distinction is one of language and culture, not of ethnicity.

note.traditional: the daily distribution; the daily ministration (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek word is the everyday term for service, including waiting on people at a meal. Most versions say “distribution” here and “ministry of the word” in verse 4, which hides the fact that Luke uses the same noun in both places and the related verb in verse 2 (“serve at tables”). The rendering keeps that thread visible: the Twelve contrast one kind of service with another. What was provided to the widows, whether food or money, is not stated.

verse.text: So the Twelve called together the community of the disciples and said, “It is not acceptable for us to abandon the word of God and serve at tables.

note.traditional: It is not right; It is not desirable

verse.note: The adjective means “pleasing” or “acceptable”, and its related verb returns in verse 5, where the proposal “was acceptable” to the community. Most versions have “not right” or “not desirable”, which loses the echo. The Greek does not say to whom it would be unacceptable; God is probably implied.

“Tables” most naturally means tables for meals, so the phrase refers to overseeing the provision of food. The same word was also used for a money-changer’s or banker’s table, and some scholars think the handling of funds is in view. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

text.q: Instead, brothers, pick out from among yourselves seven men who are well spoken of, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will put in charge of this task.
But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the service of the word.”

verse.text: The proposal was acceptable to the whole community, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte from Antioch.
verse.note: A proselyte was a Gentile who had fully converted to Judaism, which for men included circumcision. Nicolaus is the only one of the seven identified this way, implying the others were Jews by birth. All seven have Greek names, which many take as a sign that they were drawn from the Hellenist group, though Greek names were also common among Jews of Judea.

verse.text: They set these men before the apostles, and after praying they laid their hands on them.

note.term: after praying they laid their hands on them

verse.note: Grammatically the subject of “prayed” and “laid their hands” is the same as that of “set”, which is the community. Most interpreters and many translations take the apostles to be the ones who prayed and laid on hands, and that is probably what Luke means. The rendering keeps the Greek’s openness.

verse.text: And the word of God kept growing, and the number of the disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly, and a large crowd of the priests were becoming obedient to the faith.
Now Stephen, full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people.
But some of those from the synagogue called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and some of those from Cilicia and Asia, stood up and began to dispute with Stephen,

note.term: the Synagogue of the Freedmen, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians
note.traditional: the synagogue of the Libertines (KJV); the Synagogue of the Freedmen

verse.note: “Freedmen” translates a Latin loanword for former slaves or their descendants, probably Jews once taken captive to Rome and later freed. The Greek sentence can be read as naming one synagogue, two groups, or as many as five separate synagogues; the rendering takes it as one synagogue with members from Cyrene and Alexandria, plus a further group from Cilicia and Asia. “Asia” is the Roman province in what is now western Turkey.

verse.text: but they were not strong enough to stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
Then they secretly put men up to say, “We have heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God.”
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, and coming upon him they seized him and brought him to the council.
verse.note: This is the high council in Jerusalem, often called the Sanhedrin, presided over by the high priest and made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes. It is the same body before which the apostles were brought in the preceding chapters.

verse.text: They also set up false witnesses, who said, “This man never stops speaking words against the holy place and the Law,

text.q: for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will tear down this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.”

verse.text: And all who were sitting in the council looked intently at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
Then the high priest said, “Are these things so?”
He replied, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran,

text.q: and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your relatives, and come to the land that I will show you.’
Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. From there, after his father died, God resettled him in this land where you now live.
He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot of ground, yet he promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
And God spoke in this way: that his offspring would live as foreigners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave and mistreat them for four hundred years.
‘And the nation they serve as slaves I myself will judge,’ God said, ‘and after that they will come out and worship me in this place.’

verse.note: The Greek verb means religious service given to a deity, and this translation normally renders it “serve”, as in verse 42. Here “worship” is used because the same sentence already has “serve as slaves” for a different verb, and the two need to be kept apart. Most modern versions also have “worship” here; the King James Version has “serve”.

text.q: And he gave him a covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. Yet God was with him,
and rescued him from all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh king of Egypt, who appointed him governor over Egypt and over his whole household.
Then a famine came over all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food.
But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there a first time.
The second time, Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh.
Then Joseph sent and summoned his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people in all,

verse.note: The Greek counts “souls”, a Septuagint idiom for individual persons. The figure seventy-five follows the Greek version of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5; the Hebrew text has seventy.

text.q: and Jacob went down to Egypt. He died there, and so did our fathers,
and they were carried over to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.

note.term: the tomb that Abraham had bought

verse.note: In Genesis, Abraham buys a burial cave near Hebron from Ephron the Hittite, and it is Jacob who buys land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph is later buried. Stephen’s compressed summary combines the two purchases. Whether this is deliberate telescoping or reflects a different tradition is debated.

text.q: As the time drew near for the promise that God had declared to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until another king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
He dealt cunningly with our race and mistreated our fathers, making them expose their infants so that they would not survive.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in God’s sight. For three months he was raised in his father’s house,

verse.note: The Greek is literally “beautiful to God”. It may mean that God regarded the child as beautiful, or it may be a Semitic way of expressing a superlative, “exceedingly beautiful”, as when Jonah 3:3 calls Nineveh “a city great to God”. Translations are divided between the two.

text.q: and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and raised him as her own son.
So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in his words and deeds.
When he was nearing forty years of age, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel.
Seeing one of them being wronged, he came to his defense and avenged the man who was being oppressed by striking down the Egyptian.
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation through his hand, but they did not understand.
The next day he appeared to them as they were fighting and tried to reconcile them in peace, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging each other?’
But the one who was wronging his neighbor pushed him away, saying, ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’
At this word Moses fled and came to live as a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.
When forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush.
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he came near to look, the voice of the Lord came:
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.’ Moses began to tremble and did not dare to look.
Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have surely seen the mistreatment of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’
This Moses, whom they disowned, saying, ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge?’—this is the one God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’
This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers, and he received living oracles to give to us.

verse.note: This is the Greek word usually translated “church”, and the King James Version has “the church in the wilderness” here. In the Greek Old Testament it is the term for Israel gathered as a people, and a first-century hearer also knew it as an ordinary word for a civic gathering. This translation uses “assembly” everywhere so the reader can see that it is one word; most modern versions have “congregation” or “assembly” in this verse.

text.q: Our fathers were unwilling to obey him. Instead they pushed him away and in their hearts turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’
In those days they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, and they rejoiced in the works of their hands.

But God turned away and handed them over to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring me slaughtered animals and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan, the images you made in order to worship them. And I will resettle you beyond Babylon.’

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, used here for a portable shrine of Moloch and in the next verse for Israel’s wilderness sanctuary. “Tabernacle” is the traditional rendering, but it hides the plain image and the pointed contrast between the two tents. Several modern versions also use “tent”.

Verses 42–43 quote Amos 5:25–27 in its Greek version, which is where the names Moloch and Rephan come from; the Hebrew text is obscure at this point and reads differently. Amos has “beyond Damascus” in both Hebrew and Greek. Stephen’s “beyond Babylon” reflects the later exile of Judah.

text.q: Our fathers had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, just as the one who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern he had seen.
Our fathers received it in their turn and brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the land of the nations that God drove out before our fathers, until the days of David,

verse.note: In Greek the name Joshua is identical to the name Jesus, and the King James Version prints “Jesus” here. The context makes clear that Moses’ successor is meant, but a Greek reader would have heard the same name.

text.q: who found favor before God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.

verse.note: Several early and important manuscripts read “the house of Jacob” instead of “the God of Jacob”, and many scholars prefer that as the more difficult reading. The Greek text followed here reads “God”, which also matches the wording of Psalm 132:5.

text.q: But it was Solomon who built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in what is made by hands, as the prophet says:
‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?
Did not my hand make all these things?’
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become,

verse.note: This is a title for the Messiah, used also in Acts 3:14 and 22:14. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice), so the title could equally be rendered “the Just One”, as in the King James Version. In a context of betrayal and murder it also carries the sense “the innocent one”.

text.q: you who received the Law by the direction of angels and did not keep it.”

verse.note: The Greek phrase is compressed and could also be rendered “as ordinances of angels” or “as delivered by angels”. It reflects a Jewish tradition, not stated in Exodus, that angels were present and active when the Law was given at Sinai; Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2 refer to the same tradition. Here it is meant to honor the Law.

verse.text: When they heard these things, they were enraged in their hearts and ground their teeth at him.
verse.note: The verb literally means “to be sawn through”, and the traditional rendering is “cut to the heart”. In modern English that phrase suggests grief or remorse, which is what a different verb expresses in Acts 2:37. Here, as in Acts 5:33, the word describes fury, as the grinding of teeth shows.

verse.text: But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God,
and he said, “Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”
verse.note: Elsewhere the New Testament, echoing Psalm 110:1, speaks of Jesus as seated at God’s right hand. Why he is standing here is disputed: suggestions include rising to welcome Stephen, standing as his witness or advocate, or standing to judge. This is also the only place outside the Gospels where Jesus is called “the Son of Man”.

verse.text: But they cried out with a loud voice, covered their ears, and rushed at him together.
They threw him out of the city and began to stone him. And the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They went on stoning Stephen as he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Then he knelt down and cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
And Saul approved of his killing. On that day a great persecution broke out against the assembly in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader sees it is one Greek word.

verse.text: Devout men buried Stephen and made loud lamentation over him.
But Saul was ravaging the assembly: going into house after house, he dragged off both men and women and handed them over to prison.
Now those who had been scattered went from place to place announcing the good news of the word.

note.term: announcing the good news of the word

verse.note: The verb means to bring or announce good news and was an ordinary word for public announcements. Most translations have “preaching the word” or “preaching the gospel”. The same verb recurs in verses 12, 25, 35 and 40 and is rendered with “good news” each time.

verse.text: Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.
verse.note: With the article and without the name Jesus, the word here is a title: the anointed king Israel expected. Samaritans had their own hope of a coming deliverer. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as part of Jesus’ name, as in verse 12; several modern translations make the same distinction.

Some manuscripts lack the article, giving “a city of Samaria”. Which city is meant is uncertain in either case. The old capital, Samaria, had been rebuilt as Sebaste and was largely Gentile, and some scholars think another town in the region is intended.

verse.text: The crowds with one mind paid attention to what Philip was saying, as they listened and saw the signs he was doing.
For unclean spirits, shouting with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
So there was great joy in that city.
Now a man named Simon had previously been practicing magic in the city and amazing the nation of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.
verse.note: This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles”. Here it refers to the Samaritans as a distinct ethnic and religious community. They were neither Jews nor, in Jewish eyes, simply Gentiles. Most translations have “the people of Samaria”.

verse.text: All of them, from the least to the greatest, paid attention to him, saying, “This man is the Power of God that is called Great.”

note.term: the Power of God that is called Great

verse.note: The wording suggests a title: Simon was acclaimed as the embodiment or representative of the supreme divine power. “The Power” could serve as a reverent way of referring to God. Exactly what the Samaritans meant by the phrase is uncertain.

verse.text: They paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
But when they believed Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he stayed close to Philip; and seeing signs and great deeds of power taking place, he was amazed.
verse.note: The Greek word is the same one translated “Power” in verse 10 and “great” echoes the title given to Simon there, so the man hailed as the Great Power is now amazed by great deeds of power. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering, but it hides this connection.

verse.text: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,
who went down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit.
For the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
saying, “Give me this authority too, so that anyone I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter said to him, “May your silver go with you to destruction, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!

text.q: You have no part or share in this matter, for your heart is not straight before God.
So turn back from this wickedness of yours, and plead with the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.

verse.note: The verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct, here explicitly “from” something. Most translations keep “repent”, which readers generally understand to include a change of life, but in modern English it centers on feeling sorry.

text.q: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing.”

note.term: in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing
note.traditional: in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity

verse.note: Peter’s language echoes the Greek Old Testament. “Gall and bitterness” describes the person who turns from God to idolatry in Deuteronomy 29:18, and “bond of wrongdoing” appears in Isaiah 58:6. Gall is bile, a byword for anything bitter or poisonous. The preposition could also mean that Simon is heading “into” this state rather than already in it.

verse.text: Simon answered, “Plead with the Lord for me yourselves, so that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.”
So then, after they had solemnly testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they started back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news to many villages of the Samaritans.
Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Get up and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a wilderness road.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can also mean “at about noon”, which is the word’s meaning in its only other New Testament occurrence (Acts 22:6). Most translations take it as a direction, since Gaza lies southwest of Jerusalem, but a minority of scholars prefer the time reference.

The Greek says only “this is deserted” or “this is wilderness”. It may describe the road or the city of Gaza, whose old site had been destroyed and lay abandoned. It may also be either the angel’s words or the narrator’s comment; it is treated here as the narrator’s comment about the road.

verse.text: So he got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasury. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,
verse.note: “Candace” (Kandake) was not a personal name but the title of the ruling queens of the kingdom of Meroë on the upper Nile, in what is now Sudan; Greek writers called that region Ethiopia. A eunuch was barred from full membership in Israel’s assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1, though Isaiah 56:3–5 promises eunuchs a place among God’s people. The word could sometimes denote a court official without the physical sense, but Luke adds “court official” separately.

verse.text: and was now returning; sitting in his chariot, he was reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and stay close to this chariot.”
Philip ran up and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you really understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How could I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.

text.q: In his humiliation his justice was taken away. Who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 53:7–8 in the Greek version, which differs from the Hebrew. The line may mean that he was denied a fair trial, or that the sentence against him was lifted. Likewise “his generation” may refer to his contemporaries, his descendants or his origin, and “taken away from the earth” may point to his death or to his exaltation.

verse.text: The eunuch responded to Philip, “I beg you, about whom does the prophet say this—about himself or about someone else?”
Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning with this Scripture, announced to him the good news about Jesus.
As they were going along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Look, water! What prevents me from being baptized?”

note.term: What prevents me from being baptized?

verse.note: Verse 37 is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not in the Greek text translated here, so the numbering passes from 36 to 38. Some later manuscripts add: “Philip said, ‘If you believe with all your heart, you may.’ He answered, ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.’” It is generally regarded as an early addition reflecting baptismal practice.

verse.text: He ordered the chariot to stop, and both of them went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and Philip baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he traveled through he announced the good news to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.
But Saul, still breathing threat and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verse.note: In Acts “the Way” is an early name for the movement of Jesus’s followers, probably their own name for themselves. The Greek word is the ordinary one for a road or journey, and it is the same word translated “road” in verses 17 and 27.

verse.text: As he traveled, he was approaching Damascus when suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he replied, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
verse.note: The Greek form of address can mean anything from a polite “sir” to “Lord” as a divine title. Saul does not yet know who is speaking, so “sir” is possible, but the light from heaven makes clear to him that he is addressing a heavenly figure, and most translations keep “Lord.”

text.q: But get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

verse.text: The men traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either “voice” or “sound.” In Acts 22:9 Paul says his companions “did not hear the voice” of the one speaking to him, so some translations render it “hearing the sound” here to suggest they heard a noise without making out words. That distinction cannot be proved from the grammar alone, and the same word is kept as in verse 4.

verse.text: Saul got up from the ground, but though his eyes were open he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
For three days he was without sight, and he neither ate nor drank.
Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” He said, “Here I am, Lord.”
The Lord said to him, “Get up and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man from Tarsus named Saul. For look, he is praying,

text.q: and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come in and lay hands on him so that he may see again.”

verse.text: Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many people about this man, how much harm he has done to your holy ones in Jerusalem.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep; others use “God’s people.” The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the meaning here.

text.q: And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

verse.text: But the Lord said to him, “Go, because this man is my chosen instrument to carry my name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural it regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Here, set beside “the children of Israel,” it is rendered “Gentiles,” as in most translations, but “nations” is the same word and is equally possible.

text.q: For I myself will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

verse.text: So Ananias went and entered the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized,
and after taking food he regained his strength. He was with the disciples in Damascus for some days.
And immediately he began proclaiming in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

All who heard him were astonished and said, “Isn’t this the man who in Jerusalem ravaged those who call on this name? And didn’t he come here for this very purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?”
But Saul grew more and more powerful and confounded the Jews living in Damascus, proving that Jesus is the Messiah.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “the Christ.” Here the word is a title under debate in the synagogues—the anointed king Israel expected—and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and Acts, while keeping “Christ” where it functions as a name, as in verse 34.

verse.text: When a good many days had passed, the Jews plotted together to kill him,
but their plot became known to Saul. They were even watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “his disciples,” implying that Saul already had followers of his own in Damascus. Many later manuscripts read “the disciples took him,” which is smoother and may be a correction. Paul’s own account in 2 Corinthians 11:33 says he was lowered through a window in the wall.

verse.text: When he arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took hold of him and brought him to the apostles, and he related to them how on the road Saul had seen the Lord, and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.
So he stayed with them, going in and out in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He also spoke and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they were trying to kill him.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “Hellenists” (older versions: “Grecians”). The word is rare, and in Acts it most likely means Jews whose main language was Greek, as distinct from Aramaic-speaking Jews. In Acts 6:1 it refers to such Jews within the community of believers; here it refers to those outside it.

verse.text: When the brothers learned of this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
So then the assembly throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up; and living in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it grew in number.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal, and some object that “assembly” can sound like a one-off meeting. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. Many later manuscripts have the plural here, “the assemblies … had peace.”

verse.text: Now as Peter was traveling through all those parts, he came down also to the holy ones living in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a mat for eight years, for he was paralyzed.
Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.” And immediately he got up.
verse.note: The Greek says literally “spread for yourself,” without naming what is to be spread. Most translators understand it of bedding: the man is to tidy the mat he has lain on. It could also mean spreading a couch for a meal, that is, “get yourself something to eat.”

verse.text: All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
Now in Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which translated is Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity, which she did continually.
verse.note: Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas is Greek; both mean “gazelle.” Luke gives the Greek equivalent for his readers, as was common for people who moved between the two languages. The word for “disciple” here is a feminine form found nowhere else in the New Testament.

verse.text: In those days she became sick and died, and after washing her they laid her in an upstairs room.
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him to urge him, “Do not delay in coming over to us.”

So Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upstairs room, and all the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing the tunics and cloaks that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
But Peter sent them all outside, knelt down, and prayed. Then, turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
He gave her his hand and raised her up. Then he called the holy ones and the widows and presented her alive.
It became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
And Peter stayed for a good many days in Joppa with a certain Simon, a tanner.
verse.note: Tanners worked with the hides of dead animals, and the trade was foul-smelling and commonly looked down on; later Jewish tradition treats it as a despised occupation. Peter’s lodging with a tanner may quietly prepare for the next chapter, where questions of clean and unclean come to the fore.

verse.text: There was a man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of what was called the Italian Cohort,
verse.note: A cohort was a Roman army unit of several hundred soldiers, and a centurion commanded a subdivision of roughly eighty to a hundred men. Caesarea was the seat of the Roman administration of Judea. A cohort with this name is attested in the region by inscriptions, though whether it was stationed at Caesarea at this date is debated.

verse.text: a devout man who feared God along with his whole household; he did many acts of charity for the people and prayed to God continually.
verse.note: Luke uses this expression for Gentiles who worshiped Israel’s God and were attached to the synagogue without becoming full converts, which for men meant circumcision. “The people” in the same verse is Luke’s regular term for Israel, so the charity was given to Jews. Scholars debate how formal a category “God-fearers” was.

The Greek word means charitable giving to the poor, which Jewish piety ranked alongside prayer. “Alms” is accurate but has largely dropped out of ordinary English; many modern translations paraphrase with “gave generously to those in need”. The same rendering is used in verses 4 and 31.

verse.text: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God coming in to him and saying to him, “Cornelius!”
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth hour is about three in the afternoon. It was the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer in the Jerusalem temple, which suggests that Cornelius kept Jewish hours of prayer. The sixth hour in verse 9 is about noon.

verse.text: He stared at him, terrified, and said, “What is it, lord?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your acts of charity have gone up as a memorial before God.
