verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word names the portion of an offering burned on the altar so that it rises to God (as in Leviticus 2). The angel describes a Gentile’s prayers and charity in the language of temple sacrifice: they have “gone up” and been accepted.

text.q: Now send men to Joppa and send for a certain Simon, who is called Peter.
He is lodging with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.”

verse.text: When the angel who spoke to him had gone, he called two of his household slaves and a devout soldier from among those who attended him,
and after explaining everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
The next day, as they were on their way and approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray, about the sixth hour.
He became hungry and wanted to eat. But while they were preparing a meal, a trance came over him,
and he saw heaven opened and an object coming down, something like a large sheet, being lowered to the earth by its four corners.
In it were all the four-footed animals and crawling creatures of the earth and birds of the sky.
And a voice came to him: “Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.”
But Peter said, “Certainly not, Lord, for I have never eaten anything defiled or unclean.”
verse.note: The word’s everyday sense is “shared, common”, but in Jewish usage it meant ritually profane, unfit for a people set apart to God. “Common” (KJV, ESV) now suggests merely “ordinary”; other versions have “profane” or “impure”. “Defiled” follows the traditional rendering of the same word in Mark 7. The related verb in verse 15 and the adjective in verse 28 are rendered to match.

verse.text: The voice came to him again, a second time: “What God has made clean, you must not call defiled.”
This happened three times, and at once the object was taken up into heaven.
Now while Peter was at a loss within himself about what the vision he had seen might mean, just then the men sent by Cornelius, having asked their way to Simon’s house, arrived at the gate.
They called out and asked whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
While Peter was still thinking over the vision, the Spirit said to him, “There are men here looking for you.

text.q: Get up, go down, and go with them without hesitating at all, for I have sent them.”

verse.note: The verb can mean “to hesitate, to doubt” or “to make a distinction, to discriminate”. Most translations take it as hesitation here. The other sense, “making no distinction” between Jew and Gentile, is also possible and is probably in view when Peter retells the event in the next chapter.

verse.text: Peter went down to the men and said, “Here I am, the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man who fears God and is well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews, was instructed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.”
verse.note: One Greek word lies behind “nation” here and in verse 35 and “Gentiles” in verse 45. In the singular it means a people or nation, including the Jewish nation; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. English has to choose by context.

verse.text: So he invited them in and gave them lodging. The next day he got up and set out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went along with him.
On the following day he entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
As Peter was about to go in, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and paid him homage.
verse.note: The verb means to prostrate oneself in reverence, and what the gesture signifies depends on who receives it. Most translations have “worshiped” here, and Peter’s reply shows he considered the reverence excessive for a mere human. Since Cornelius, a worshiper of Israel’s God, is unlikely to have taken Peter for a deity, “paid him homage” is used; some scholars think Luke does intend an improper act of worship.

verse.text: But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a human being.”
Talking with him, he went in and found many people gathered.
He said to them, “You yourselves know how forbidden it is for a Jewish man to associate with or visit someone of another people. But God has shown me that I should call no person defiled or unclean.
verse.note: The word describes what offends against established custom or sacred order, something taboo, and is not the usual term for breaking a written law. No commandment in the Law of Moses prohibits visiting a Gentile; the restriction arose from purity concerns, especially about food, and was observed with varying strictness. “Unlawful” could suggest a scriptural rule that did not exist.

text.q: That is why I came without objection when I was sent for. So I ask, for what reason did you send for me?”

verse.text: Cornelius said, “Four days ago, at this very hour, I was in my house praying at the ninth hour, and suddenly a man in shining clothing stood before me

note.term: Four days ago, at this very hour
note.traditional: Four days ago I was fasting until this hour

verse.note: The Greek is awkward, literally “from the fourth day until this hour I was praying the ninth”. Most interpreters take it to mean that the vision came four days earlier at the same hour of the day, the ninth. Many later manuscripts add that Cornelius was fasting, which is the reading behind the KJV.

text.q: and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your acts of charity have been remembered before God.
So send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’
So I sent to you at once, and you were kind enough to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you.”

verse.text: Then Peter opened his mouth and said, “In truth, I am grasping that God shows no partiality,

text.q: but in every nation the one who fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.
You know the word that he sent to the children of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all.

note.term: You know the word that he sent

verse.note: The grammar of verses 36–38 is broken in Greek, and translators must supply connections. Here “the word” is taken as a first object of “you know” in verse 37, so the verb is repeated. Others link it back to verse 34 or treat it as a loose heading (“As for the word…”), and some manuscripts omit “that”, giving “He sent the word to the children of Israel”. The overall sense is not affected.

text.q: You yourselves know what took place throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed:
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.
We are witnesses of everything he did, both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. And they put him to death by hanging him on a tree.

verse.note: The Greek word means wood or anything made of it: a beam, a stake, or a tree. It refers here to the cross, and the phrase echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where a body hung “on a tree” is under God’s curse. “Tree” is kept so that the scriptural allusion can be heard.

text.q: God raised him on the third day and granted that he be plainly seen,
not by all the people but by witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand—by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
He commanded us to proclaim to the people and to testify solemnly that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.
To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”

verse.text: While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening to the word.
The believers from among the circumcised, all who had come with Peter, were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles too,
for they heard them speaking in tongues and praising the greatness of God. Then Peter responded,

text.q: “Can anyone withhold the water and keep these people from being baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?”

verse.text: And he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay on for some days.
Now the apostles and the brothers and sisters throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” Jewish writers used its plural for all the peoples other than Israel. This translation renders the same word “Gentiles” where non-Jews are meant and “nations” where peoples as such are in view.

verse.text: But when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took issue with him,

note.traditional: they that were of the circumcision

verse.note: Literally “those of circumcision.” The phrase may mean simply Jewish believers, which at this point is nearly everyone in the Jerusalem community. It may instead mean a group within it that insisted on circumcision and separation from Gentiles. The Greek does not settle which.

verse.text: saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”
But Peter began and laid it all out for them in order, saying,

text.q: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: something like a large sheet coming down, lowered from heaven by its four corners, and it came right up to me.
I stared at it and looked closely, and I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the crawling things, and the birds of the sky.
I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.’
But I said, ‘Certainly not, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’

verse.note: The word ordinarily meant “shared” or “ordinary.” Jewish Greek used it for what is ritually profane, such as food unfit for a people set apart to God. The verb in verse 9, “treat as common,” is built on the same word, so the voice turns Peter’s own term back on him.

text.q: But a voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, you must not treat as common.’
This happened three times, and then everything was pulled up again into heaven.
And at that very moment three men arrived at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.
The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also came with me, and we entered the man’s house.

verse.note: The same verb can mean “hesitate” or “doubt,” and many translations render it so here, matching the parallel at 10:20. The form here is active, which favors “making no distinction,” that is, between Jew and Gentile. The same verb is translated “took issue” in verse 2, so Peter’s critics are doing what the Spirit told him not to do. Manuscripts vary in the wording of this phrase.

text.q: He reported to us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter;
he will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning.
And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he used to say, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
So if God gave them the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”

verse.text: When they heard this, they fell silent. Then they glorified God, saying, “So then, God has given even to the Gentiles the turning back that leads to life.”
verse.note: Most translations keep “repentance,” understood to include a change of life. In current English, “repentance” centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct.

verse.text: Now those who had been scattered by the affliction that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verse.note: Most translations have “persecution” here, which fits the events of chapter 8. The Greek is the general word for hardship pressing on people from outside, and this translation renders it “affliction” throughout so the reader can see it is one word.

verse.text: But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and began to speak to the Greek speakers as well, announcing the good news of the Lord Jesus.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between “Hellenists” (Greek speakers), the reading translated here, and the plain word “Greeks.” In 6:1 the first word refers to Greek-speaking Jews. Here the contrast with “Jews” in verse 19 shows that non-Jews are meant on either reading, and most scholars agree on that sense.
Older translations have “preaching the Lord Jesus.” The verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news publicly. Many modern translations also render it “good news” here.

verse.text: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
The report about them reached the ears of the assembly in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas out as far as Antioch.
verse.note: “Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” wherever the word occurs.

verse.text: When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he urged them all to remain true to the Lord with resolute hearts,
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a large crowd was added to the Lord.
Then he went off to Tarsus to look for Saul,
and when he found him he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they gathered with the assembly and taught a large crowd, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
verse.note: The name is formed the way party labels were formed, meaning roughly “Christ’s people” or “partisans of Christ.” The verb can mean to bear a name publicly. Most scholars think outsiders in Antioch coined the label, though this is not certain. The word is rare in the New Testament, appearing elsewhere only at Acts 26:28 and 1 Peter 4:16.

verse.text: In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come over the whole inhabited world—and this took place under Claudius.
verse.note: The term means the inhabited world and was often used loosely for the Roman Empire. Claudius was emperor from AD 41 to 54. Ancient sources record repeated food shortages during his reign, including a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s.

verse.text: So the disciples decided, each according to their means, to send relief to the brothers and sisters living in Judea.
This they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
About that time King Herod laid hands on some who belonged to the assembly, to do them harm.
verse.note: This is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and nephew of the Herod Antipas who appears in the Gospels. He ruled Judea as king under Roman patronage from AD 41 until his death in AD 44, which helps date the events of this chapter.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” everywhere the word occurs, so that the reader sees one Greek word.

verse.text: He had James the brother of John killed with the sword.
When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread.
Having seized him, he put him in prison, handing him over to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover.

note.term: four squads of four soldiers each

verse.note: Sixteen soldiers in all, probably one squad of four for each of the four watches of the night. Verse 6 fits this, with two soldiers chained to Peter and two on guard at the door.

Luke uses “Passover” for the whole week-long festival, including the days of Unleavened Bread mentioned in verse 3. Herod intended to wait until the festival was over before staging a public trial. The King James Version’s “Easter” here is an anachronism.

verse.text: So Peter was kept in the prison, but prayer for him was being earnestly made to God by the assembly.
When Herod was about to bring him out, that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards in front of the door kept watch over the prison.
And suddenly an angel of the Lord stood there, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly!” And the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, “Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.” And he did so. Then he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”
He went out and followed, and he did not know that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.

After passing the first guard post and the second, they came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened for them by itself. They went out and walked the length of one street, and immediately the angel left him.
When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s hand and from everything the people of the Jews were expecting.”
When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was also called Mark, where a good number had gathered and were praying.
When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer,
verse.note: In this period the word normally meant a female slave, not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servant girl” or “maid.” A household large enough to host a gathering and to have a gateway would ordinarily have owned slaves.

verse.text: and recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gateway but ran in and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gateway.
They said to her, “You are out of your mind!” But she kept insisting that it was so. And they kept saying, “It is his angel.”
verse.note: Many Jews of the period believed that a person had a guardian angel, and some later sources suggest such an angel could resemble the person. The speakers assume that what stands at the gate is this heavenly counterpart, not Peter himself. Some interpreters think they mean that Peter has been killed and that this is his spirit, but the word does not normally mean “ghost.”

verse.text: But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened they saw him and were astounded.

Motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Report these things to James and the brothers and sisters.” Then he left and went to another place.
verse.note: This is not James the brother of John, who was killed in verse 2. It is James the brother of Jesus, who appears from this point on as the leading figure in the Jerusalem assembly (Acts 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19).

The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address or refer to a mixed group of fellow members, and the gathering in this house included women. “Brothers” is the traditional rendering; many recent versions use “brothers and sisters” or “believers.”

verse.text: When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
Herod searched for him and did not find him; he interrogated the guards and ordered them led away to execution. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.
verse.note: The Greek says only that Herod ordered the guards “to be led away.” The verb was a common idiom for taking someone off to execution, and under Roman practice a guard who lost a prisoner could suffer the prisoner’s penalty, so most translators understand it that way. It could mean only that they were led off to prison.

verse.text: Now he was furious with the people of Tyre and Sidon. But with one mind they came to him, and having won over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country was fed from the king’s.
On an appointed day Herod, dressed in royal robes and seated on the platform, was delivering a public address to them,
and the populace kept shouting, “The voice of a god, not of a human being!”
verse.note: The Greek has no article, and the crowd in Caesarea is largely pagan, so “a god” is the natural sense. Honoring rulers as divine was common in the eastern Roman world. “The voice of God” is grammatically possible but less likely on these speakers’ lips.

verse.text: Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died.
verse.note: The same verb describes the angel striking Peter to wake him in verse 7; the repetition is probably deliberate, one blow rescuing and the other judging. The Jewish historian Josephus independently records that Agrippa, hailed as more than mortal in Caesarea, did not reject the flattery, was seized by violent abdominal pain and died some days later. Luke’s account is compressed and need not mean that he died on the spot.

verse.text: But the word of God kept growing and multiplying.
Barnabas and Saul returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem, taking along with them John, who was called Mark.
verse.note: The best-attested reading is “to Jerusalem,” which is difficult because Barnabas and Saul were already there (11:30) and next appear in Antioch (13:1). Other manuscripts read “from Jerusalem,” probably a scribal correction, and most English versions follow them. The edition translated here keeps “to Jerusalem” but punctuates so that the phrase goes with the service, which this translation renders “their service in Jerusalem”; the return is then to Antioch.

The word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf; here it is the delivery of famine relief from Antioch (11:29–30). Older versions have “ministry” and many modern ones “mission.” “Service” avoids the clerical overtone of “ministry” and keeps the link with the related words for “serve” and “servant.”

verse.text: Now in Antioch, in the assembly there, were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius the Cyrenian, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “church.” A first-century hearer knew the word as a gathering of people—a civic assembly, or in the Septuagint Israel assembled before God—whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. Nearly all translations keep “church,” which readers readily understand; “assembly” is used here throughout so that the one Greek word stays visible.

verse.text: While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Now set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
So these two, sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
Arriving in Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They also had John as an assistant.
When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they found a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. The proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the magician—for that is how his name is translated—opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked straight at him
and said, “You who are full of all deceit and all villainy, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not stop twisting the straight ways of the Lord?
verse.note: Greek has a single word family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” and the verb “justify.” “Righteousness” is kept here, as in most English translations, though some scholars prefer “justice.” The verb of this family appears in verses 38–39 as “justified,” where “justified from” carries the sense of being cleared of a charge and so released from it.

verse.text: And now look, the hand of the Lord is against you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell on him, and he went around looking for people to lead him by the hand.
Then the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Paul and his companions put out to sea from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John, however, left them and returned to Jerusalem.
But they went on from Perga and arrived at Pisidian Antioch. On the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent word to them: “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, speak.”
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said, “Israelites, and you who fear God, listen.
verse.note: Besides Jews by birth, synagogues in the Greek cities attracted Gentiles who worshiped Israel’s God and kept some Jewish practices without becoming full converts. Paul addresses them alongside the Israelites here and again in verse 26. How formal or uniform a group these “God-fearers” were is debated.

text.q: The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and lifted up the people during their stay as foreigners in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm he led them out of it.
And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness,

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter: “he put up with them” and “he cared for them,” as a nurse carries a child. The same variation is found in the Greek text of Deuteronomy 1:31, which Paul echoes here. The evidence is closely balanced and translations differ; the text followed here reads “put up with.”

text.q: and after overthrowing seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave their land as an inheritance,

verse.note: The Greek word translated “nations” here is the same word translated “Gentiles” in verses 46–48. It means a people or nation, and in the plural it often refers to the non-Jewish peoples as a whole. The translation chooses between the two English words according to the sense.

text.q: all of this over about four hundred and fifty years. After that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.

note.term: all of this over about four hundred and fifty years
note.traditional: and after that he gave them judges for about four hundred and fifty years

verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts the four hundred and fifty years belong with what precedes, apparently covering the stay in Egypt, the wilderness years and the conquest. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, place the figure after the giving of judges, making it the length of the judges’ period. The words “all of this” make the reference of the earlier reading clear.

text.q: Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
After removing him, he raised up David as their king, and bore witness about him, saying, ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will carry out all my wishes.’
From this man’s offspring God, as he promised, has brought to Israel a savior, Jesus.
Before his arrival, John had already preached to all the people of Israel a baptism of turning back.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term understood to include a change of life. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct.

text.q: And as John was completing his course, he would say, ‘What do you suppose I am? I am not he. But look, one is coming after me, and I am not worthy to untie the sandals on his feet.’
Brothers, sons of Abraham’s family, and those among you who fear God, it is to us that the word of this salvation has been sent.
For the people living in Jerusalem and their rulers, failing to recognize him or to understand the voices of the prophets that are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him.
Though they found no grounds for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him put to death.
When they had carried out everything that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now his witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news of the promise made to the fathers:
God has fulfilled it for our children by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have become your Father.’

verse.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read “for our children,” which fits the context awkwardly, since Paul is speaking of his own generation. Other manuscripts read “for us, their children” or “for their children,” and many translations adopt “for us, their children.” Some scholars suspect an early copying error behind all the surviving readings.

This may mean raising Jesus from the dead, as the same verb plainly does in verse 34, or raising him up in the sense of bringing him onto the stage of history, as Scripture speaks of God raising up a prophet. Interpreters are divided, and the rendering leaves both possibilities open.

text.q: And as for his raising him from the dead, never again to return to decay, he has spoken in this way: ‘I will give you the holy and faithful things of David.’

note.term: the holy and faithful things of David
note.traditional: the sure mercies of David; the holy and sure blessings of David

verse.note: The quotation follows the Greek version of Isaiah 55:3, where the Hebrew speaks of God’s reliable acts of loyal love toward David. The Greek is terse—“the holy things of David, the faithful ones”—and translations usually supply a noun such as “blessings” or “promises.” The plain wording is kept so that the link with “your Holy One” in the next verse, which is the same Greek word, remains visible.

text.q: That is why he also says in another place, ‘You will not let your Holy One see decay.’
For David, after serving God’s purpose in his own generation, fell asleep and was gathered to his fathers and saw decay,

note.term: after serving God’s purpose in his own generation

verse.note: The Greek can be construed in more than one way: “after serving God’s purpose in his own generation,” “after serving his own generation by God’s purpose,” or “after serving his own generation, fell asleep by God’s purpose.” Translations are divided. The contrast with Jesus, who did not see decay, is unaffected.

text.q: but the one whom God raised did not see decay.
So let it be known to you, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and that from everything from which you could not be justified by the Law of Moses,
by this man everyone who believes is justified.
Take care, then, that what is said in the Prophets does not come upon you:
‘Look, you scoffers, be amazed and vanish, for I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe even if someone tells you of it.’”

verse.text: As Paul and Barnabas were going out, the people begged that these things be spoken to them on the next Sabbath.
When the synagogue meeting had broken up, many of the Jews and the devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke with them and urged them to continue in the grace of God.
On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they contradicted what Paul was saying, hurling insults.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “blaspheming.” In first-century Greek the verb meant abusive or defamatory speech against anyone, not only against God, and no object is stated here; many modern translations have “reviling him” or “heaped abuse on him.” Some interpreters do read it as blasphemy against Christ.

verse.text: Then Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly and said, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. Since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look, we are turning to the Gentiles.
verse.note: In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of its kind as well as its length. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators render “the life of the age to come.”

text.q: For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the end of the earth.’”

verse.text: When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who had been appointed to eternal life believed.
verse.note: The verb means to assign, arrange or appoint, and the form here is most naturally read as a passive, “had been appointed,” with God as the implied agent; this is the majority view. Some take it instead as “had set themselves” toward eternal life, in contrast to those in verse 46 who judged themselves unworthy of it. The text does not say when or on what basis the appointing took place.

verse.text: And the word of the Lord spread through the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, raised a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their territory.
So they shook the dust off their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
In Iconium the same thing happened: they went into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.

note.traditional: they went together into the synagogue

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean either “in the same way”—that is, as had just happened in Pisidian Antioch—or “together.” Older versions and some recent ones take it as “together”; others read it as here. Both fit the context, and the choice is not certain.

verse.text: But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish way of referring to the non-Jewish peoples. It is rendered “Gentiles” here and in verses 5 and 27, and “nations” in verse 16, where all the world’s peoples are in view. It is the same word throughout.

verse.text: So they spent a considerable time there, speaking boldly in reliance on the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done through their hands.
But the people of the city were divided: some were with the Jews and others with the apostles.
verse.note: Only here and in verse 14 does Acts call Paul and Barnabas “apostles”; elsewhere in the book the term is kept for the Twelve. The word meant an envoy sent on someone’s behalf, and many scholars think it is used here of the two as delegates sent out by the assembly in Antioch (13:1–3), though this is debated.

verse.text: When a move was made by both Gentiles and Jews, together with their leaders, to mistreat them and stone them,
they learned of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the surrounding region,
and there they went on announcing the good news.
verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or a book title, so the plain sense is given here, as many modern translations also do.

verse.text: In Lystra there sat a man who had no strength in his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked.
This man listened to Paul as he spoke. Paul looked intently at him and, seeing that he had faith to be healed,
verse.note: The verb covers both physical healing and “being saved” in the fuller religious sense, and Luke often plays on the two. The immediate reference is to the man’s lameness, so “healed” is used, but a first-century reader would have heard the wider sense as well.

verse.text: said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” And he sprang up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices and said in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in human form!”
They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the one who took the lead in speaking.
verse.note: Zeus was the chief of the Greek gods and Hermes their messenger and spokesman, which is why Paul, as the speaker, is taken for Hermes. The Roman poet Ovid tells a story set in neighboring Phrygia in which Zeus and Hermes visit the region disguised as humans, which may explain the crowd’s reaction. Older English versions use the Latin names Jupiter and Mercury.

verse.text: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood just outside the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and, together with the crowds, wanted to offer sacrifice.
But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting,
verse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a Jewish gesture of grief or horror, used especially on hearing blasphemy. Paul and Barnabas react this way once they understand that they are about to be worshiped as gods; the delay is probably because the crowd had been speaking Lycaonian.

text.q: “Men, why are you doing this? We too are human beings, with the same nature as you, and we are bringing you the good news that you should turn from these worthless things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.

verse.note: The word means empty, futile or useless, and the Septuagint uses it as a dismissive term for idols and foreign gods. “Vanities” now suggests conceit to most readers, so “worthless things” is used. The reference is to the gods and the sacrifice being prepared.

text.q: In past generations he allowed all the nations to go their own ways.
Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good: he gave you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, and filled your hearts with food and gladness.”

verse.text: Even with these words they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
But Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium, and after winning over the crowds they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing that he was dead.
But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and went into the city. The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
After they had announced the good news to that city and made a good many disciples, they returned to Lystra, to Iconium, and to Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples and urging them to remain in the faith, saying, “It is through many afflictions that we must enter the kingdom of God.”
verse.note: The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that presses on people. “Tribulation” is now often heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word does. Other versions have “hardships” or “persecutions.”

verse.text: And when they had appointed elders for them in each assembly, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The verb was used both of electing by a show of hands and, more generally, of appointing or choosing. Here Paul and Barnabas are the subject, so “appointed” is the natural sense. Whether the local believers had a part in the choice is not stated.

verse.text: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia,
and after speaking the word in Perga they went down to Attalia,
and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
verse.note: Two different cities named Antioch appear in this chapter. In verses 19 and 21 it is Antioch near Pisidia, in central Asia Minor. Here it is Antioch in Syria, the city from which Paul and Barnabas had been sent out (13:1–3).

verse.text: When they arrived, they gathered the assembly and reported all that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they spent no little time with the disciples.
Some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”

When this brought Paul and Barnabas into no small conflict and debate with them, they arranged for Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them to go up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and elders, about this question.
So, sent on their way by the assembly, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, telling in detail of the conversion of the Gentiles, and they brought great joy to all the brothers.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” remains the near-universal rendering, and readers should understand “assembly” here as the community of believers, not a single meeting.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural in Jewish usage it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses “Gentiles” for that sense and “nations” elsewhere, but it is one word. In verse 14 James plays on it: God takes from the “nations” a “people,” the term normally reserved for Israel.

verse.text: When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.
But some from the party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to command them to keep the Law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders gathered to look into this matter.

After much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the good news and believe.
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or a book title; the Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

text.q: And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us,
and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
So now why are you putting God to the test by laying on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we have had the strength to bear?

verse.note: The verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel testing God in the wilderness. “Tempt” in modern English means to entice to sin, which is not the idea here; most recent versions also use “test.”

text.q: No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are.”

verse.text: The whole community fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul recounting all the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
When they had fallen silent, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me.

text.q: Simeon has recounted how God first concerned himself to take from the Gentiles a people for his name.

verse.note: This is a Semitic form of the name Simon and refers to Simon Peter, who has just spoken. The form suits a speaker from the Aramaic-speaking community in Jerusalem.

The verb is the Septuagint’s regular word for God “visiting” his people to act for them. Here it has no personal object and is completed by “to take a people,” so “visited” would require supplying words. English versions divide between “visited the Gentiles,” “concerned himself,” “looked favorably,” and “intervened.”

text.q: And with this the words of the prophets agree, as it is written:
‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and set it upright again,

verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for a tent or hut. The image is of David’s royal house as a collapsed shelter that God will rebuild. Older versions have “tabernacle”; several modern ones already use “tent” or “dwelling.”

text.q: so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who makes these things

note.term: so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord
note.traditional: that the residue of men might seek after the Lord

verse.note: James quotes Amos 9:11–12 in a form close to the ancient Greek translation, with some wording that differs from it. The Hebrew text of Amos reads differently here: “that they may possess the remnant of Edom.” The Greek version, with all humanity seeking the Lord, is the one that carries James’s argument.

note.term: over whom my name has been called
note.traditional: who are called by my name

verse.note: The Greek reproduces a Hebrew idiom in which calling one’s name over something marks it as one’s own property. The traditional rendering suggests only that the Gentiles bear God’s name; the idiom says they belong to him.

text.q: known from of old.’

note.traditional: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world

verse.note: The words can be read as “who makes these things known from of old” or as “who does these things, which have been known from of old”; the translation allows the first and the Greek permits either. Many later manuscripts expand the phrase into a separate sentence, which the King James Version follows; the shorter text is generally judged original.

text.q: Therefore I judge that we should not make difficulties for those from the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but should write to them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood.

verse.note: This refers to meat from animals killed without draining the blood. The four prohibitions are often thought to echo the rules that Leviticus 17–18 lays on foreigners living among Israel, though this is debated; others see them as matters associated with pagan worship. Some manuscripts of the Western tradition omit “what has been strangled” here and in verse 29 and add a negative form of the Golden Rule, turning the list into moral rules.

text.q: For Moses from ancient generations has had in every city those who proclaim him, since he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

verse.text: Then the apostles and the elders, together with the whole assembly, resolved to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers.
verse.note: The Greek expression, used here and in verses 25 and 28, is the standard formula with which Greek cities and councils recorded official decisions. “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (verse 28) is the familiar rendering and is literal, but in English it sounds tentative where the Greek states a formal resolution.

verse.text: They wrote this to be delivered by their hand: “The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers from among the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: Greetings.

text.q: Since we have heard that some who went out from us have disturbed you with their words and unsettled your minds, though we gave them no instructions,

verse.note: The Greek word covers a person’s life and inner self. Here it is the seat of conviction that the visitors have unsettled, for which “minds” is the natural English; most modern versions agree. The same word is rendered “lives” in verse 26.

text.q: we have resolved, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means “hand over.” With “their lives” as object, most translations understand it as exposing their lives to danger, but it can also be read as “devoted their lives.” The same verb appears in verse 40, where the brothers hand Paul over to the Lord’s grace, rendered there “entrusted.”

text.q: So we have sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For the Holy Spirit and we have resolved to lay on you no further burden than these necessary things:
to abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.”

verse.text: So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, and after gathering the community they delivered the letter.
When they read it, they rejoiced at the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, who were themselves also prophets, encouraged the brothers at length and strengthened them.
After spending some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.

note.term: to those who had sent them

verse.note: Verse 34 (“But it seemed good to Silas to remain there”) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not part of the Greek text translated here. It was probably added by copyists to explain how Silas could be in Antioch in verse 40.

verse.text: But Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and, along with many others, bringing the good news of the word of the Lord.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Come, let us go back and visit the brothers in every city where we announced the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing.”
Barnabas wanted to take along John, called Mark, as well,
but Paul thought it right not to take along this man, who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work.
The disagreement became so sharp that they parted from each other: Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus,
while Paul chose Silas and set out, entrusted by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
He passed through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
He also came to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple named Timothy was there, the son of a believing Jewish woman but of a Greek father,
and he was well spoken of by the brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address or describe a mixed group of men and women, and here it means the members of the believing community. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; several recent ones use “brothers and sisters” or “believers.” In verse 40 the group meets in Lydia’s house and plainly includes women.

verse.text: Paul wanted this man to set out with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they traveled through the cities, they handed on to them the decrees decided on by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to keep.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for handing something into another’s keeping, and it is also used for passing on teaching or instructions. Most versions have “delivered”; “handed on” keeps the link with the same verb elsewhere. The “decrees” are the decisions of the Jerusalem meeting in the previous chapter.

verse.text: So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith and grew in number day by day.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used of civic assemblies and, in the Greek Old Testament, of Israel gathered before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is visible wherever it appears.

verse.text: They went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.

note.traditional: Phrygia and the region of Galatia

verse.note: The Greek can be read as one district (the part of Phrygia lying within the Roman province of Galatia) or as two (Phrygia, and Galatian territory farther north). The choice bears on the long-running debate over where the Galatian assemblies were, and scholars remain divided. “Asia” here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, not the continent.

verse.text: When they came up to Mysia, they tried to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.
So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.
During the night a vision appeared to Paul: a Macedonian man was standing there, pleading with him and saying, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to set out for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to bring the good news to them.
verse.note: Here the narrative shifts without explanation from “they” to “we,” the first of several such passages in Acts. The usual explanation is that the author, or a source he used, joined Paul’s party at Troas; some scholars regard the first-person plural as a literary convention. The “we” drops away after Philippi and resumes in chapter 20.

The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has since become a religious term and a book title, so this translation uses “good news.” Many modern versions already alternate between the two.

verse.text: So we put out to sea from Troas and ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of that district of Macedonia, a colony. We stayed in this city for some days.

note.term: a leading city of that district of Macedonia
note.traditional: the chief city of that part of Macedonia

verse.note: The text translated is the reading of the principal manuscripts. It is awkward historically, since Philippi was the capital neither of the province nor of its own district, and so some editions adopt a conjecture, “a city of the first district of Macedonia.” Macedonia had been divided into four districts by the Romans. “A leading city” takes the Greek as a claim to prominence and not to capital status.

Luke uses the Latin word in Greek letters. A Roman colony was a settlement, often of army veterans, whose citizens held Roman citizenship and lived under Roman law and Roman-style magistrates. This explains the accusers’ appeal in verse 21 to what is lawful “for us” as Romans.

verse.text: On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.
verse.note: The Greek word for “prayer” was also a regular term for a Jewish meeting place, sometimes a building and sometimes an open-air site, often near water. The fact that only women are mentioned may suggest that Philippi had no established synagogue. Some manuscripts read “where prayer was customarily offered.”

verse.text: A woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God, was listening, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.
verse.note: In Acts this expression regularly describes Gentiles who attached themselves to the synagogue and worshiped Israel’s God without becoming full converts. Lydia was probably such a person and not Jewish by birth. Thyatira, in the province of Asia, was known for its dyeing trade, and purple cloth was a luxury product.

verse.text: When she and her household had been baptized, she pleaded with us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” And she prevailed on us.
Once, as we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl who had a spirit of divination met us. She brought her owners a great deal of profit by fortune-telling.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “a spirit, a python.” Python was the serpent of Delphi in Greek myth, slain by Apollo, whose oracle there was the most famous in the Greek world; by this period the word was used for a spirit believed to speak predictions through a person, and for such soothsayers themselves. A first-century reader would have understood that the girl was regarded as an oracle.

verse.text: She followed after Paul and us, crying out, “These men are slaves of the Most High God, and they are proclaiming to you a way of salvation.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and not for a hired servant. Most translations soften it to “servants.” In the Greek Old Testament “slave of God” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and the prophets. The word is pointed on the lips of a girl who is herself owned.

The Greek has no article, so the phrase can be read as “a way” or “the way” of salvation. “Most High God” was a title Jews used for the God of Israel, but Gentiles also used it for Zeus or another supreme deity, and “salvation” could mean rescue or well-being of many kinds. To a crowd in Philippi the girl’s cry was therefore open to a pagan understanding, which may be part of why Paul is exasperated.

verse.text: She kept doing this for many days. But Paul, exasperated, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to go out of her.” And it went out that very hour.
When her owners saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the authorities,
and bringing them to the magistrates they said, “These men are throwing our city into turmoil; they are Jews,
verse.note: The Greek word, literally “generals,” was the standard Greek equivalent for the pair of chief magistrates who governed a Roman colony. They are probably the same officials as “the authorities” in verse 19, now named by their title.

text.q: and they are proclaiming customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans.”

verse.text: The crowd joined in the attack on them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off them and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison, commanding the jailer to guard them securely.
Having received such a command, he threw them into the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the jail were shaken. At once all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and seeing the doors of the prison open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out in a loud voice, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”
The jailer asked for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them outside and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
verse.note: The jailer’s respectful address is the plural of the word translated “Lord” in the reply of verse 31 and “owners” in verses 16 and 19. A Greek reader would have heard the echo: he addresses them as lords, and they point him to the Lord Jesus.

verse.text: They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.
At that hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds, and he and all who were his were baptized at once.
He brought them up into his house and set a meal before them, and he rejoiced with his whole household that he had come to believe in God.
When day came, the magistrates sent the lictors, saying, “Release those men.”
verse.note: The Greek word means “rod-bearers” and was the regular term for Roman lictors, the attendants who walked before a magistrate carrying a bundle of rods as the sign of his authority and who carried out his sentences. The verb for “beaten with rods” in verse 22 is from the same root, so these are presumably the men who did the beating. “Police” suggests a modern institution that did not exist.

verse.text: The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent word that you are to be released. So come out now and go in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “They beat us in public without a trial, men who are Romans, and threw us into prison, and now they are throwing us out in secret? No indeed! Let them come themselves and bring us out.”
verse.note: “Romans” here means holders of Roman citizenship, not natives of Rome. Roman law protected citizens from being beaten or imprisoned without trial, and officials who violated that protection could face serious consequences, which explains the magistrates’ fear in verse 38. There is irony in the charge of verse 21, where the accusers set themselves as Romans against Paul and Silas as Jews.

verse.text: The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans.
So they came and pleaded with them, and after bringing them out they kept asking them to leave the city.
After coming out of the prison they went to Lydia’s house, and when they had seen the brothers and sisters they encouraged them and departed.
After traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
As was his custom, Paul went in to them, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
explaining and setting out that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I am proclaiming to you, is the Messiah.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the title of the anointed king Israel expected. Where that title is itself the point under discussion, as in Paul’s synagogue argument here, this translation uses “Messiah”; where the word works as a name alongside “Jesus,” it keeps “Christ.” Several modern translations make the same split.

verse.text: Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a large number of the Greeks who worshiped God and not a few of the leading women.
verse.note: Luke uses “those who worship” almost as a label for non-Jews who attended the synagogue and honored Israel’s God without becoming full converts. The same group appears in verse 17. They were often among the first to respond to Paul’s message.

verse.text: But the Jews grew jealous, and taking along some bad characters from among the marketplace loafers, they formed a mob and set the city in an uproar. They descended on Jason’s house, seeking to bring them out before the people’s assembly.
When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some brothers before the city magistrates, shouting, “These men who have stirred up unrest across the world are now here as well,

note.term: stirred up unrest across the world

verse.note: The verb is used of political agitation and revolt; Luke uses it again of a rebel leader in Acts 21:38. The traditional phrase has become almost a compliment in English, but in the accusers’ mouths it is a charge of sedition, which fits the accusation about Caesar that follows. “World” here is the inhabited world, in practice the Roman empire.
Luke uses the specific title “politarchs.” It is attested in inscriptions as the title of the chief magistrates in Macedonian cities, including Thessalonica.

text.q: and Jason has taken them in. They are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”

verse.text: They agitated the crowd and the city magistrates as they heard these things,
and after taking a bond from Jason and the others, the magistrates released them.
The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. When they arrived, they went into the synagogue of the Jews.
These were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures every day to see whether these things were so.
Many of them therefore believed, as did not a few of the Greeks—women of high standing as well as men.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in Berea as well, they came there too, stirring up and agitating the crowds.
Then the brothers immediately sent Paul away to go as far as the sea, but Silas and Timothy both stayed there.
Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving instructions for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they left.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and those who worshiped God, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also debated with him. Some said, “What is this scavenger of scraps trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign deities.” This was because he was announcing the good news about Jesus and the resurrection.
verse.note: The word was used of birds that pick up seed, and then as an insult for someone who picks up scraps of other people’s ideas and passes them off as learning. “Babbler” suggests mere chatter; the sneer is rather that Paul is a second-hand dabbler with no real philosophy. Standard lexicons offer glosses such as “scrapmonger.”

On Greek lips this word means divine beings in general, not “demons” as elsewhere in the New Testament. The charge recalls the famous accusation against Socrates of introducing new divinities to Athens. Some interpreters think the hearers took “Jesus and Resurrection” (Anastasis in Greek) for a pair of deities; this is possible but uncertain.
The Greek verb was an ordinary word for publicly announcing good news. “Gospel” has become a religious term in English, so this translation uses “good news,” as many modern versions do.

verse.text: They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
verse.note: The name means “Hill of Ares,” a rocky rise below the Acropolis, and it also names the ancient Athenian council that originally met there and that still had standing in religious and civic matters in Roman times. It is disputed whether Paul was taken to the hill for an informal hearing or brought before the council. “In the midst of the Areopagus” (verse 22) and the mention of Dionysius “the Areopagite,” a council member (verse 34), favor the council, though Luke does not describe a formal trial.

text.q: For you are bringing some strange things to our ears, so we want to know what these things mean.”

verse.text: Now all the Athenians and the foreigners staying there used to spend their time on nothing other than telling or hearing the latest thing.
Then Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.
verse.note: The Greek word can be approving (“devout toward the gods”) or disparaging (“superstitious”). At the opening of a speech seeking a hearing, the neutral or complimentary sense is the more likely, and most modern translations take it so. Luke’s readers, having been told of Paul’s distress at the idols, may also have heard the double edge.

text.q: For as I walked around and looked carefully at your objects of worship, I even found an altar with the inscription ‘To an unknown god.’ So what you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by hands,
nor is he served by human hands as if he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and everything.
From one he made every nation of humankind to live on the whole face of the earth, having determined prescribed times and the boundaries of where they would live,

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “from one blood,” which the King James Version follows. The earliest witnesses have simply “from one,” and SBLGNT prints that. The phrase most naturally refers to one man, Adam, though the Greek does not say so explicitly.

text.q: so that they would seek God, if perhaps they might grope for him and find him—though he is in fact not far from each one of us.
For in him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’

verse.note: The quoted line comes from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a poet from Cilicia, Paul’s home region; in the poem “his” refers to Zeus. A very similar line occurs in Cleanthes’ Hymn to Zeus, which may explain the plural “poets.” The preceding words, “in him we live and move and exist,” are sometimes attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides, but that attribution is uncertain.

text.q: Since then we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, something carved by human skill and imagination.
God has overlooked the times of ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to turn back,

verse.note: “Repent” in modern English centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets’ call to “return” to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct; here it means turning from idols to the living God. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term.

text.q: because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world with justice by a man he has appointed, giving proof to all by raising him from the dead.”

verse.note: Greek has one word family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). This translation normally uses “righteousness,” but here the subject is fair judging, so “justice” is used. The phrase echoes the Psalms, where God “will judge the world in righteousness” (for example Psalm 96:13; 98:9).

The Greek noun is the one this translation normally renders “faith.” Here it stands in a set expression, “to furnish pistis,” which in the Greek of the period meant to supply a pledge or proof, and “faith” would not make sense in English. A minority of interpreters read “offering faith to all,” but the idiom is well established and most translations render “proof” or “assurance.”

verse.text: When they heard of a resurrection of the dead, some began to scoff, but others said, “We will hear you about this again.”
So Paul went out from their midst.
But some men attached themselves to him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, and also a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to see them,
and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
verse.note: The word is rare, and its exact scope is uncertain. Many scholars think it covered leatherworking more broadly, since tents were often made of leather; others think of weaving tent-cloth. “Tentmakers” is kept as the plain sense of the word.

verse.text: Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul gave himself wholly to the word, testifying solemnly to the Jews that the Messiah was Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered “Christ.” Here and in verse 28 it is a title under debate in the synagogue—the anointed king Israel expected—so “Messiah” is used, as several modern translations do in such places. The word order suggests the question was who the Messiah is, with “Jesus” as the answer, though “that Jesus was the Messiah” is also possible.

verse.text: But when they opposed him and hurled insults, he shook out his clothes and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
verse.note: In first-century Greek this verb meant abusive speech against anyone, not only against God, whereas English “blaspheme” is now limited to irreverence toward the divine. With no object stated, the natural sense is abuse directed at Paul. Some interpreters, however, understand the abuse as aimed at Christ, and so as blasphemy in the stricter sense.

Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off and disowning responsibility. Paul’s words echo the watchman of Ezekiel 33, who is clear of guilt once he has given warning; “your blood be on your own heads” means that the responsibility for what follows is theirs.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations.” In the plural it was the ordinary Jewish way of referring to the non-Jewish peoples, and it is rendered “Gentiles” in that sense. It is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere in the New Testament.

verse.text: Then he moved on from there and went into the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
verse.note: In Acts this expression regularly describes a non-Jew who attached himself to the synagogue and honored Israel’s God without becoming a full convert. Paul’s move next door, into a Gentile’s house, puts into action his words in verse 6.

verse.text: Crispus, the synagogue leader, believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians, as they heard, believed and were baptized.
One night the Lord said to Paul in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent,

text.q: for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for there are many in this city who are my people.”

verse.text: So he settled there for a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal,
verse.note: Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca, governed the Roman province of Achaia, whose capital was Corinth. An inscription found at Delphi places his term of office in about AD 51–52, which makes this episode one of the most securely dated points in Paul’s life. The “tribunal” was the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases.

verse.text: saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.”
verse.note: The accusers do not say whether they mean Roman law or the Jewish Law, and the vagueness may be deliberate. Gallio takes it as the latter (“your own law,” verse 15) and so dismisses the case as an internal religious dispute.

verse.text: Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were some crime or serious wrongdoing, Jews, it would be reasonable for me to bear with you.

text.q: But if these are questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I am not willing to be a judge of such things.”

verse.text: And he drove them away from the tribunal.
Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the tribunal; and none of this mattered to Gallio.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts say only “all” and do not identify the attackers. Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “the Greeks,” making this a bystanders’ assault on a Jewish leader; a few others read “the Jews,” as if the accusers turned on their own spokesman. Either is possible, and the text leaves it open.

verse.text: Paul stayed on for a good many days more, then took leave of the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. At Cenchreae he had his hair cut off, for he was under a vow.
verse.note: The Greek plural, grammatically masculine, was the ordinary way of addressing or naming a mixed group of men and women. Here it refers to the whole community of believers at Corinth, so “brothers and sisters” is used, as in several recent translations. Others keep “brothers.”

note.term: he had his hair cut off

verse.note: In the Greek the phrase follows directly after the name Aquila, and grammatically it could refer to him. Most interpreters take it of Paul, the subject of the sentence. The vow is not explained; cutting the hair recalls the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, though there the hair was cut at the temple, so the exact practice here is uncertain. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port.

verse.text: They arrived at Ephesus, and there he left them. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay longer, he did not consent,
but took his leave, saying, “I will come back to you again, God willing.” Then he set sail from Ephesus,

note.term: “I will come back to you again, God willing.”
note.traditional: I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem: but I will return again unto you, if God will

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have Paul first say that he must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem. The earliest manuscripts lack these words. Most scholars regard them as a later addition, perhaps made to explain his haste.

verse.text: and after landing at Caesarea he went up and greeted the assembly, and then went down to Antioch.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal and familiar. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Scriptures’ term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” everywhere, so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The Greek does not name the place. “Going up” and “going down” were the standard expressions for traveling to and from Jerusalem, and most interpreters understand that Paul went up from the port of Caesarea to greet the assembly in Jerusalem before going on to Antioch. A minority take it to mean only that he went up from the harbor to the assembly in Caesarea.

verse.text: After spending some time there he set out and traveled from place to place through the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, arrived in Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, powerful in the Scriptures.
verse.note: The word can mean either “eloquent” or “learned,” and translations are divided. Alexandria was famous for both rhetoric and scholarship, and the two senses overlap, since ancient education centered on skill in speech. “Eloquent” is chosen because his knowledge of the Scriptures is mentioned separately.

verse.text: He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
