He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
When he wanted to cross over to Achaia, the brothers and sisters encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. On arriving, he was a great help to those who had believed through grace,
for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing through the Scriptures that the Messiah was Jesus.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the inland regions and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples
and said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered him, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”

note.term: that there is a Holy Spirit
note.traditional: whether there be any Holy Ghost

verse.note: The Greek says literally “whether there is a Holy Spirit.” Since disciples of John the Baptist would have known of God’s Spirit from Scripture and from John’s own preaching, many interpreters take the sense to be “whether the Holy Spirit has been given” (compare John 7:39, where similar wording has that meaning). The translation keeps the plain wording and leaves the question open.

verse.text: He said, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John baptized with a baptism of turning back, telling the people to believe in the one coming after him—that is, in Jesus.”
verse.note: Most translations have “a baptism of repentance.” In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most versions keep “repentance” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying.
There were about twelve men in all.
He went into the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading people about the kingdom of God.

But when some became hardened and would not be persuaded, speaking evil of the Way in front of the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples aside, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
verse.note: The ordinary word for “road” or “way” is used in Acts as a name for the movement of Jesus’s followers (also 9:2; 19:23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). It is capitalized here because it functions as a name.

verse.text: This went on for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
God was doing no ordinary deeds of power through the hands of Paul,
verse.note: The Greek is the plural of the ordinary word for “power,” used of concrete acts that display it. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and is used by most versions; “deeds of power” is chosen so that the link with “power” elsewhere stays visible. The phrase “no ordinary” reproduces Luke’s deliberate understatement.

verse.text: so that even face cloths or work aprons that had touched his skin were carried off to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.

Then some of the Jewish exorcists who traveled from place to place also tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
verse.note: No high priest named Sceva is known from other sources. The title may mean that he belonged to one of the high-priestly families, or it may be a title he or his sons claimed in order to impress clients; exorcists valued any link to the Jerusalem temple and its sacred names. Luke reports the title without comment.

verse.text: But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know about; but you—who are you?”
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them all, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
verse.note: The Greek word normally means “both,” which sits awkwardly with the seven sons of verse 14. In later everyday Greek it could be used loosely for “all,” and most translators take it that way here. The alternative is that only two of the seven were involved in this incident.

verse.text: This became known to all who lived in Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.
Many of those who had come to believe kept coming, confessing and disclosing their practices.
A good number of those who had practiced magic brought their scrolls together and burned them in front of everyone. They added up their value and found it came to fifty thousand silver coins.
verse.note: The coin is not named, but it is probably the drachma, roughly a laborer’s daily wage. The sum is therefore very large. Ephesus was well known in antiquity for written spells and magical formulas, and the scrolls burned were presumably collections of these.

verse.text: So the word of the Lord kept growing mightily and prevailing.

note.term: the word of the Lord kept growing mightily
note.traditional: So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed

verse.note: The Greek word order is unusual and can be read two ways: “the word of the Lord grew mightily” or “by the might of the Lord the word grew.” The translation follows the first, the reading of most versions, taking the phrase as the common idiom for “with force.” The verb “prevailing” echoes verse 16, where the possessed man “prevailed against” the exorcists.

verse.text: When these things had been completed, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go on to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
verse.note: The phrase can mean that Paul made up his own mind (“resolved in his spirit”) or that he decided under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Translations are divided. The following “I must,” and the later statement that he goes to Jerusalem “bound by the Spirit” (20:22), favor the second reading, but the first is entirely possible.

verse.text: He sent two of his assistants, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed on for a time in Asia.
About that time no small disturbance arose concerning the Way.
A man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought the craftsmen no small amount of business.
He gathered them together, along with the workers in related trades, and said, “Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business.

text.q: And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

The danger is not only that this trade of ours will come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she whom all Asia and the world worship will even be stripped of her majesty.”

verse.text: When they heard this they were filled with rage and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed as one into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s traveling companions.
Paul wanted to go in before the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the leading officials of Asia, who were his friends, sent word to him and urged him not to venture into the theater.
verse.note: The Greek title is “Asiarchs,” which some translations simply carry over; others have “the chief of Asia” or “officials of the province.” Asiarchs were wealthy, prominent men of the province of Asia who held or had held high public office; their exact duties and their connection with the provincial council and the imperial cult are debated. Luke’s point is that Paul had friends at the highest level of local society.

verse.text: Some were shouting one thing and some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together.
verse.note: This is the same Greek word that elsewhere in the New Testament names the community of believers, traditionally translated “church.” Here it has its ordinary civic meaning, a gathering of citizens, and in verse 39 it refers to the city’s regular, legally constituted meeting. This translation uses “assembly” for the word everywhere so that the reader can see it is one word.

verse.text: Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had pushed forward, and Alexander motioned with his hand, wanting to make a defense before the people.

note.traditional: they drew Alexander out of the multitude

verse.note: The meaning of the verb here is uncertain, and manuscripts vary. It may mean that some of the crowd instructed or prompted Alexander, or that they concluded Alexander was the cause of the trouble; other manuscripts read that he was pushed forward or brought down out of the crowd. It is also unclear whether the Jews put him forward to distance themselves from Paul.

verse.text: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, a single cry went up from them all, and for about two hours they shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

When the city clerk had calmed the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, what person is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple guardian of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky?
verse.note: Elsewhere in the New Testament this word means a scribe, an expert in the Jewish Law. In a Greek city of Asia it was the title of the chief civic official, who drafted decrees, presided at the citizens’ assembly, and answered to the Roman authorities for public order. That explains his alarm in verse 40.

note.term: the image that fell from the sky
note.traditional: the image which fell down from Jupiter

verse.note: The Greek has a single adjective meaning “fallen from Zeus” or “fallen from the sky,” with no noun; “image” or “sacred stone” is supplied. It probably refers to a sacred object, possibly a meteorite, kept in the temple and believed to be of heavenly origin. “Temple guardian” was an honorific title that cities claimed, attested for Ephesus on inscriptions and coins.

text.q: Since these things are undeniable, you ought to stay calm and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here, though they are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So then, if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a case against anyone, the courts are in session and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another.
But if you are seeking anything beyond this, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.

verse.text: For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, since there is no cause for it, and we will not be able to give an account of this disorderly gathering.” And having said this, he dismissed the assembly.

note.term: And having said this, he dismissed the assembly.

verse.note: Some editions and translations number this final sentence as verse 41; the Greek edition followed here includes it in verse 40. The Greek of the clerk’s last sentence is also tangled, and manuscripts differ over whether a “not” belongs in it, though the general sense is clear: the city could give no justification for the commotion if called to account.

verse.text: After the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples, and when he had encouraged them and said farewell, he set out to go to Macedonia.
After he had gone through those parts and encouraged them with many words, he came to Greece,
where he spent three months. When the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Beroea, by Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, by Gaius from Derbe and Timothy, and by Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
These men arrived and waited for us at Troas.
verse.note: The Greek text translated here has a verb meaning “came” or “arrived.” Many manuscripts, followed by most English versions, have a verb differing by a single letter that means “went ahead.” On either reading this group reached Troas before the narrator’s party did.

The narrative shifts here into the first person plural, last used at Philippi (16:10–17). The usual explanation is that the author, or a source he drew on, rejoined Paul’s company at this point. The origin and significance of these “we” passages are debated.

verse.text: But we sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and within five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was speaking to them. Because he was going to leave the next day, he kept talking until midnight.

note.term: On the first day of the week

verse.note: The Greek is a Jewish idiom, literally “on day one of the Sabbaths,” meaning the first day of the week. It is uncertain whether Luke is counting days from sunset, in the Jewish way, which would make this Saturday night, or from morning, which would make it Sunday night. This is among the earliest references to believers gathering on that day.

verse.text: There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window, sinking into a deep sleep as Paul went on speaking still longer. Overcome by sleep, he fell from the third story to the ground below and was picked up dead.
But Paul went down, threw himself on him, and put his arms around him, and said, “Stop this commotion, for his life is in him.”
verse.note: The verb describes noisy tumult and is related to the noun rendered “uproar” in verse 1. It is used elsewhere of the loud wailing of mourners (Mark 5:39), which fits the scene here. Most translations take it as inward alarm, which is also possible.

verse.text: Then he went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked with them a long while, until dawn; and so he left.
They brought the boy away alive and were not a little comforted.
We, meanwhile, went ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, where we intended to take Paul on board; for he had arranged it so, intending to go there by land himself.
When he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we arrived the next day off Chios; the day after, we crossed over to Samos, and on the day following we came to Miletus.
For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not have to spend time in Asia; he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if he possibly could, on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the assembly.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering, as in the previous chapter, and the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one word.

verse.text: When they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia,

text.q: serving the Lord with all humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews;
how I did not hold back from declaring to you anything that would benefit you, or from teaching you in public and from house to house,
testifying to both Jews and Greeks about turning back to God and faith in our Lord Jesus.

verse.note: Most translations have “repentance,” an established term understood to include a change of life. In current English, however, that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct.

text.q: And now, look, bound by the Spirit I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will meet me there,

verse.note: The Greek can mean that Paul is constrained by the Holy Spirit or that he feels bound in his own spirit, that is, inwardly compelled. Most modern translations take it of the Holy Spirit, as here; older versions took it of Paul’s spirit. “Bound” anticipates the “chains” of the next verse, a related word in Greek.

text.q: except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in city after city, saying that chains and afflictions await me.
But I do not count my life as worth anything or as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of the grace of God.

verse.note: Most translations have “ministry” here. The Greek was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests a clerical profession.

The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, including public proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title. Many modern translations already alternate between the two.

text.q: And now, look, I know that none of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will see my face again.
Therefore I bear witness to you this very day that I am clean of the blood of all,
for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.
Pay close attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God, which he acquired through his own blood.

verse.note: The men addressed are the same people called “elders” in verse 17. The Greek word later came into English as “bishop,” but here it describes the elders’ function of watching over the community, not a separate rank.

The Greek can also be read “through the blood of his Own,” that is, of his own Son, and a number of scholars and some translations prefer this because speaking of God’s blood is so unusual. The rendering here follows the more ordinary grammar of the phrase. Some manuscripts read “the assembly of the Lord” in place of “the assembly of God,” which would remove the difficulty; “of God” is generally judged more likely to be original.

text.q: I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock,
and from among your own selves men will rise up and speak twisted things, to draw the disciples away after them.
Therefore stay alert, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been made holy.

verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and means to bring someone into the sphere of what belongs to God. Most translations use “sanctified,” which hides that link and now suggests to many readers a technical doctrine of gradual moral improvement. The meaning itself is not in dispute.

text.q: I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands provided for my own needs and for those who were with me.
In everything I showed you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said,
‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

note.term: It is more blessed to give than to receive

verse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in any of the four Gospels. Paul cites it as something his hearers are expected to know already, which shows that sayings of Jesus circulated apart from the written Gospels.

verse.text: When he had said this, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
They all wept a great deal, and they threw their arms around Paul’s neck and kissed him,
grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they were never going to see his face again. Then they escorted him to the ship.
When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.
We came in sight of Cyprus and, leaving it on our left, sailed on to Syria and put in at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.
We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.
When our days there were up, we left and went on our way, and all of them, with wives and children, escorted us until we were outside the city. There we knelt on the beach and prayed
and said farewell to one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they returned to their homes.
We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais, and after greeting the brothers and sisters we stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.
verse.note: These are the seven men chosen in Acts 6 to oversee the daily distribution of food in Jerusalem. This Philip later proclaimed the message in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (Acts 8), and he is distinct from Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve.

verse.text: He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we were staying there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “This is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is and hand him over into the hands of Gentiles.’”
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” In the plural it regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples and is then rendered “Gentiles.” It is the same word in verses 19, 21 and 25.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody. Older versions have “deliver,” and many recent ones have “hand over” here. Luke uses the same verb for Jesus being handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32), and the echo is probably intended.

verse.text: When we heard this, both we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
Since he would not be persuaded, we said no more except, “Let the Lord’s will be done.”
After these days we got ready and began the journey up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us, bringing us to Mnason, a Cypriot and an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
verse.note: The Greek is compressed and can also be read as “bringing with them Mnason, with whom we were to lodge,” as some older versions have it. Most modern translations take it as here. “Early disciple” probably means he had belonged to the movement from its first days.

verse.text: When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went in with us to see James, and all the elders were present.
verse.note: This is James the brother of Jesus, by this time the leading figure in the Jerusalem community (Acts 12:17; 15:13; Galatians 1:19). He is not James the son of Zebedee, whose death is reported in Acts 12:2.

verse.text: After greeting them, he recounted one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his service.
verse.note: Most translations have “ministry.” In the first century this was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession.

verse.text: When they heard this, they glorified God, and they said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law.

text.q: But they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to the customs.
What, then, is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow they took of their own accord.

verse.note: The head-shaving and the offerings point to a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which ended with shaving the head and costly sacrifices. Paying for the sacrifices of others who had taken such a vow was a recognized act of piety. Exactly how Paul’s own purification and the seven days of verse 27 fit the procedure is debated.

text.q: Take these men, be purified along with them, and pay their expenses so that they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also stay in line and keep the Law.

As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent word of our decision that they should keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

verse.text: Then Paul took the men, and on the next day, after being purified along with them, he went into the temple to give notice of when the days of purification would be completed and the offering presented for each one of them.
When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him,
verse.note: “Asia” here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, not the continent. Its chief city was Ephesus, where Paul had worked for several years, which is why these Jews recognized both Paul and Trophimus the Ephesian.

verse.text: shouting, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the Law and this place. What is more, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”
verse.note: Non-Jews could enter the outer court of the temple, but a barrier marked the point beyond which they were forbidden to go on pain of death. Greek inscriptions warning of this have been found. The charge, which verse 29 calls a mistaken assumption, was therefore a capital one.

verse.text: For they had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was aroused, and the people came running together. They took hold of Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, a report went up to the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
verse.note: The Greek title, literally “leader of a thousand,” was the standard equivalent of the Roman military tribune. Here it is the officer in charge of the cohort stationed in Jerusalem, a unit of several hundred to a thousand soldiers. The garrison was housed in the Antonia fortress, which overlooked the temple courts and was joined to them by steps, so the report “went up” and the troops “ran down.”

verse.text: At once he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the commander came up, took hold of him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains; and he began asking who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. Since he could not learn anything certain because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the mass of the people followed, shouting, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the commander, “May I say something to you?” He replied, “Do you know Greek?

text.q: Then you are not the Egyptian who some time ago raised a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”

verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin word sicarii, “dagger-men.” It names militants who killed their opponents in crowds with concealed daggers. Josephus also describes an Egyptian prophet who led a large following in the time of the governor Felix and escaped when the Romans attacked. The commander’s words are best read as a surprised inference from Paul’s Greek, though some take them as a question expecting the answer yes.

verse.text: Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he had given permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. When a great silence had fallen, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
verse.note: The phrase may mean Hebrew itself or Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea, which Greek writers could also call “Hebrew.” Many scholars and several translations take it as Aramaic; others argue that Hebrew is meant. The translation keeps the Greek’s own term.

text.q: “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make to you.”

verse.text: When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said:
verse.note: The Greek says literally “the Hebrew dialect.” Many scholars think this means Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea, which Greek writers of the period did not always distinguish from Hebrew. Others hold that Hebrew itself is meant. The text keeps the Greek term and leaves the question open.

text.q: “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated strictly according to the Law of our ancestors, and zealous for God, just as all of you are today.

note.traditional: brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel

verse.note: To sit at a teacher’s feet is to be his pupil; Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and teacher of the Law in Jerusalem (Acts 5:34). The punctuation is uncertain: the phrase can go with what precedes, as here, or with what follows (“brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel”). Either way Paul claims a Jerusalem upbringing and a strict training in the Law.

text.q: I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prisons,

verse.note: In Acts “the Way” is a name for the movement of Jesus’s followers (for example Acts 9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14). The Greek word is the ordinary one for a road or path.

text.q: as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. From them I even received letters to the brothers in Damascus, and I was traveling there to bring those who were there as well to Jerusalem, bound, to be punished.

verse.note: Here “the brothers” are fellow Jews in the synagogues of Damascus, not followers of Jesus. Paul is speaking as a Jew to a Jewish crowd, whom he has just addressed as “brothers and fathers.”

text.q: As I was on my way and coming near Damascus, about midday a great light from heaven suddenly flashed around me,
and I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me,
‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me,
‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’

verse.note: The Greek word can be a polite “sir” or the title “Lord.” Paul does not yet know who is speaking, but he is answering a voice from heaven, so “Lord” is kept, as in most translations.

text.q: Those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me.

note.traditional: heard not the voice; some versions “did not understand the voice”

verse.note: Acts 9:7 says Paul’s companions heard the voice but saw no one. Some translations reconcile the two accounts by rendering this verse “did not understand the voice,” appealing to a difference in Greek case; most grammarians doubt that the distinction holds. The text translates the verb in its ordinary sense and leaves the tension visible.

text.q: I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me,
‘Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.’
Since I could not see because of the glory of that light, I came into Damascus led by the hand by those who were with me.
A certain Ananias, a man devout according to the Law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,
came to me, stood beside me, and said to me, ‘Brother Saul, regain your sight!’ And at that very moment I regained my sight and saw him.

note.traditional: receive thy sight ... I looked up upon him

verse.note: The Greek verb means both “look up” and “see again,” and it is used twice here: Ananias’s command and Paul’s response are the same word. The second occurrence, which is followed by “at him,” could also be rendered “I looked up at him.”

text.q: He said, ‘The God of our ancestors has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear the voice from his own mouth,

note.traditional: the Just One; the Righteous One

verse.note: A title for the Messiah, used also in Acts 3:14 and 7:52. The Greek adjective covers what English divides among “righteous,” “just” and “innocent.”

text.q: because you will be a witness for him to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’
When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me,
‘Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’
And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I was imprisoning and beating those who believed in you.
And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing there, approving, and guarding the cloaks of those who were killing him.’
And he said to me,
‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it names the non-Jewish peoples. It is this statement—that the risen Jesus sent Paul away from Jerusalem to non-Jews—that ends the crowd’s willingness to listen.

verse.text: They listened to him up to this statement; then they raised their voices and said, “Away from the earth with such a man! It is not right for him to live!”
As they were shouting, throwing off their cloaks, and flinging dust into the air,
the commander ordered him to be brought into the barracks and said he was to be interrogated under the lash, so that he could find out why they were shouting against him like this.
verse.note: The Greek title, literally “leader of a thousand,” was the standard Greek equivalent for a Roman military tribune, here the officer commanding the cohort garrisoned in Jerusalem. Many translations use “tribune”; “commander” is used here because the same Greek word also serves for senior officers in general.

verse.text: But when they had stretched him out with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and has not been condemned?”

note.traditional: bound him with thongs; stretched him out for the whips

verse.note: The Greek can mean that Paul was stretched out and tied “with the straps,” or stretched out “for the lashes,” that is, for the whipping. The word usually means a leather strap or thong, and a different word is used for the whip in verse 24, so the first reading is followed here. Many translations take the second.

The Greek says simply “a Roman,” which in this context means a holder of Roman citizenship, not someone from Rome. Roman law protected citizens from being flogged without trial, and an officer who violated this could be held to account, which is why the soldiers back away at once.

verse.text: When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and reported it, saying, “What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen.”
The commander came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” He said, “Yes.”
The commander answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum of money.” Paul said, “But I was born a citizen.”
So those who were about to interrogate him withdrew from him at once, and the commander too was afraid when he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him.

The next day, wanting to know for certain what he was being accused of by the Jews, he unbound him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and stood him before them.
Looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have conducted my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.”
verse.note: The verb originally described living as a citizen and discharging public duties, and some translations bring that out (“fulfilled my duty to God”). By this period it was also used more generally for how a person conducts his life, especially in Jewish Greek writing about living by God’s law. The rendering keeps the more general sense; a civic overtone is possible but cannot be shown.

verse.text: But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me according to the Law, and yet in violation of the Law you order me to be struck?”
verse.note: The image is of a shaky wall given a coat of whitewash to hide its condition, and many scholars hear an echo of Ezekiel 13:10–15, where God promises to bring such a wall down. Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest from about AD 47 to 59. Ordering an accused man struck before any finding of guilt went against the Law’s demand for fair judgment.

verse.text: Those standing by said, “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”
Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”
verse.note: It is disputed whether Paul means this literally (the hearing was irregular, convened by a Roman officer, and he may not have recognized who gave the order) or ironically, implying that a man who behaves this way is not acting as a high priest. The Greek allows either. The quotation is from Exodus 22:28.

verse.text: Realizing that one faction was made up of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, Paul cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.”

note.term: the hope and the resurrection of the dead
note.traditional: the hope and resurrection of the dead

verse.note: The Greek joins two nouns with “and.” Many interpreters take this as a single idea, “the hope of the resurrection of the dead,” and several translations render it that way. The text keeps the two nouns as the Greek has them; the sense is much the same either way.

verse.text: As he was saying this, a conflict broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was split.
For Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but Pharisees affirm them all.
verse.note: The Greek word normally means “both,” but in the Greek of this period it could be used of more than two (as in Acts 19:16). If it means “both” here, the two things are resurrection on one side and angel-or-spirit on the other. Some scholars instead read “angel” and “spirit” as describing forms of the resurrected state that the Sadducees denied.

verse.text: A great outcry arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ faction stood up and argued fiercely, saying, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit has spoken to him, or an angel—”

note.traditional: let us not fight against God

verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts the sentence breaks off unfinished, as if drowned out by the uproar. Later manuscripts complete it with “let us not fight against God,” probably borrowed from Acts 5:39; the King James Version follows that longer text.

verse.text: As the conflict grew fierce, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn apart by them, ordered the troops to go down, snatch him from among them, and bring him into the barracks.
verse.note: The Greek title, literally “commander of a thousand,” was the standard equivalent of the Roman military tribune. This officer commanded the cohort stationed in the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple, which is the “barracks” of this chapter. Some translations use the more general “commander.”

verse.text: The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage! For just as you have testified fully about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify in Rome as well.”
When day came, the Jews banded together and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
verse.note: Many modern translations say the men took an “oath,” but the verb is stronger: they called down a curse on themselves, declaring themselves devoted to destruction, if they failed to carry out the vow. The older English tradition (“bound themselves under a curse”) is closer to the Greek. In verse 14 the Greek doubles the word for emphasis, rendered there as “a solemn curse.”

verse.text: There were more than forty who formed this conspiracy.
They went to the chief priests and the elders and said, “We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

text.q: So now you, together with the council, notify the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to examine his case more closely. As for us, we are ready to kill him before he gets near.”

verse.text: But the son of Paul’s sister heard about the ambush, and he came and entered the barracks and reported it to Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.”
So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “The prisoner Paul called me over and asked me to bring this young man to you, since he has something to say to you.”
The tribune took him by the hand, drew him aside privately, and asked, “What is it that you have to report to me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

text.q: So do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him. They have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him, and now they are ready, waiting for your promise.”

verse.text: So the tribune dismissed the young man, ordering him, “Tell no one that you have notified me of this.”
Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get two hundred soldiers ready to go as far as Caesarea, along with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, starting at the third hour of the night.
verse.note: The meaning of this word is uncertain. It is found nowhere else in surviving Greek of this period and only rarely centuries later. It seems to name some kind of light-armed soldier; “spearmen” is the conventional guess, and others have suggested slingers, bowmen or local auxiliaries.

note.term: the third hour of the night
note.traditional: the third hour of the night

verse.note: Night hours were counted from sunset, so this is about nine in the evening. The size of the escort, nearly half the garrison, shows how seriously the tribune took the threat.

text.q: Provide mounts as well, so that they can put Paul on them and bring him safely through to Felix the governor.”

verse.text: He wrote a letter to this effect:

text.q: “Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix: greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

note.term: having learned that he was a Roman citizen
note.traditional: having learned that he was a Roman

verse.note: The letter presents events in the order most flattering to its writer. According to Acts 21:31–39 and 22:24–29, Lysias learned of Paul’s citizenship only after he had arrested him, put him in chains and ordered him flogged, none of which the letter mentions.

text.q: Wanting to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.
I found that he was being accused over disputed points of their law, but faced no charge deserving death or chains.
When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, and I also ordered his accusers to state their case against him before you.”

verse.note: Many later manuscripts close the letter with the customary “Farewell.” The earliest witnesses lack it, and the SBLGNT omits it.

verse.text: So the soldiers, in keeping with their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
The next day they let the horsemen go on with him and returned to the barracks.
When the horsemen entered Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.
After reading it, he asked what province he was from, and on learning that he was from Cilicia, he said,
“I will hear your case when your accusers have arrived as well.” Then he ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod’s praetorium.
verse.note: A praetorium was the official residence and headquarters of a Roman governor. In Caesarea the governors used the palace built by Herod the Great, so Paul was held in the governor’s own compound, not in a common prison. Felix’s question about Paul’s province in verse 34 was to establish whether he had jurisdiction over the case.

verse.text: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate, a certain Tertullus, and they presented their case against Paul to the governor.
verse.note: The Greek word means a trained public speaker, and in a courtroom setting it was the ordinary term for a professional who pleaded cases for clients. “Orator” now suggests a maker of fine speeches, not legal counsel, so “advocate” is used; other modern versions have “attorney” or “lawyer”.

verse.text: When Paul had been called in, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Because of you we enjoy great peace, and through your foresight reforms are being made for this nation.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles”. In the singular it means a people or nation, and in this chapter (verses 2, 10 and 17) it refers to the Jewish people.

text.q: In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we welcome this with all gratitude.

verse.note: Speeches before a Roman official conventionally opened with compliments designed to win the judge’s goodwill, and “most excellent” was the standard form of address for a governor. Tertullus’s praise is formula, not description: other ancient sources portray Felix’s governorship as harsh and marked by unrest.

text.q: But so as not to detain you any longer, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.
For we have found this man to be a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.

verse.note: The Greek word meant a school of thought or party and is used elsewhere in Acts of the Pharisees and Sadducees without any negative sense. It had not yet acquired the later meaning “heresy”, though Tertullus uses it dismissively and Paul in verse 14 declines the label. “Nazarenes” as a name for the followers of Jesus of Nazareth occurs only here in the New Testament.

text.q: He even tried to desecrate the temple, and we seized him.

verse.note: Verse 7 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not included in the Greek text translated here. Later manuscripts add, from the end of verse 6 to the start of verse 8, “and wanted to judge him according to our law. But the tribune Lysias came and with great violence took him out of our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you.” With the longer text, “from him” in verse 8 could refer to Lysias instead of Paul.

text.q: By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about all these things we accuse him of.”

verse.text: The Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.
When the governor nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I gladly make my defense.

text.q: As you are able to find out, it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
They did not find me debating with anyone or stirring up a crowd—not in the temple, not in the synagogues, not anywhere in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things they are now accusing me of.
But this I admit to you: according to the Way, which they call a sect, I serve the God of our ancestors, believing everything that accords with the Law and everything written in the Prophets,

verse.note: “The Way” is the name Acts uses for the movement of Jesus’s followers as they themselves spoke of it (also in verse 22). Paul’s point is that it is not a breakaway party but the right way of serving Israel’s God in keeping with the Scriptures.

Most English versions have “worship” here. The Greek verb means to render religious service to a god, whether by rites or by a whole life of devotion, and it is a different word from the one translated “worship” in verse 11, which names the act of bowing in reverence. “Serve” keeps the two apart.

text.q: and having a hope in God, which these men themselves also hold, that there is going to be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.
For this reason I too always strive to keep a clear conscience before God and people.
Now after several years I came to bring gifts for the poor to my nation, and to present offerings.

verse.note: The traditional “alms” is accurate but has largely dropped out of modern English. The word means charitable gifts to those in need. This is probably a reference to the collection Paul gathered from his largely Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem, which his letters discuss at length but Acts mentions only here.

text.q: While I was occupied with these, they found me in the temple, ritually purified, with no crowd and no uproar.
But there were some Jews from Asia—they are the ones who ought to be here before you to accuse me, if they have anything against me.
Or let these men themselves say what crime they found when I stood before the council,
unless it was this one thing I shouted as I stood among them: ‘It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

verse.text: But Felix, who was rather accurately informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.”
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody, but to allow him some freedom and not to prevent any of his own people from attending to his needs.
Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
verse.note: Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I (the Herod of Acts 12) and sister of the Agrippa and Bernice who appear in chapter 25. According to the Jewish historian Josephus, Felix persuaded her to leave her first husband, the king of Emesa, to marry him. This gives point to Paul’s chosen topics in verse 25.

verse.text: But as Paul discussed righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and answered, “Go away for now; when I find an opportunity, I will send for you.”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Here the word may mean right conduct in general or, since Felix was a judge who hoped for a bribe (verse 26), “justice” in the narrower sense; some translations choose the latter. The same family lies behind “the righteous and the unrighteous” in verse 15.

verse.text: At the same time he was also hoping that Paul would give him money; for that reason he sent for him quite often and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and wanting to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
verse.note: The two years are most naturally those of Paul’s custody in Caesarea, and this is the usual view. A minority of scholars take the phrase to refer to the length of Felix’s term as governor. The date of Festus’s arrival is itself uncertain, usually placed between AD 55 and 60.

verse.text: So Festus, three days after arriving in the province, went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem,
and the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews laid charges against Paul before him. They kept urging him,
asking as a favor against Paul that he send for him to come to Jerusalem—they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.
Festus replied that Paul was being held at Caesarea and that he himself intended to leave for there soon.
“So let the men of standing among you come down with me,” he said, “and if there is anything improper about the man, let them accuse him.”
After spending no more than eight or ten days among them, he went down to Caesarea, and the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought in.
verse.note: The word names the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases; a ruling given from it was official. “Judgment seat” is the older English rendering, and several modern versions already use “tribunal.” Taking his seat there marks the hearing as a formal trial.

verse.text: When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they were unable to prove,
while Paul said in his defense, “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar.”
But Festus, wanting to do the Jews a favor, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges before me?”
Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

text.q: If, then, I am in the wrong and have done something deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”

note.term: hand me over to them as a favor

verse.note: Most versions say “give me up” or “hand me over.” The Greek verb means to grant something as a favor, and it echoes the noun “favor” in verses 3 and 9: Paul is saying that he is not a gift the governor may make to his accusers. The same verb is used in verse 16.

A Roman citizen facing a capital charge in the provinces could ask to have his case transferred to the emperor’s court in Rome. Once the appeal was accepted, the governor could no longer dispose of the case himself. “Caesar” is the emperor’s title; the emperor at this time was Nero.

verse.text: Then Festus, after conferring with his council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”
After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
verse.note: This is Herod Agrippa II, son of the Herod whose death is told in Acts 12 and great-grandson of Herod the Great. Bernice was his sister. He ruled territories to the north and east under Roman patronage and had the right to appoint the Jewish high priest, which is why Festus treats him as an expert on Jewish matters.

verse.text: Since they were staying there for several days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man here whom Felix left behind as a prisoner.

text.q: When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid charges against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him.

I answered them that it is not the custom of Romans to hand over any person as a favor before the accused has faced his accusers in person and has had the opportunity to defend himself against the charge.
So when they assembled here, I allowed no delay: the next day I took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought in.
When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge against him of the kind of crimes I had suspected;

note.term: the kind of crimes I had suspected

verse.note: The manuscripts differ over the word rendered “crimes” here: it appears in more than one grammatical form, and some manuscripts lack it altogether. The sense is little affected either way—the accusers brought none of the charges Festus had expected.

text.q: instead they had some disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died but whom Paul claimed was alive.

verse.note: The Greek word can be neutral (“religion,” “reverence for the divine”) or dismissive (“superstition”), and older versions chose the latter. Since Festus is speaking courteously to a Jewish king, the neutral sense is more likely, and most modern translations agree. “Their own” could also be read as “his own,” meaning Paul’s.

text.q: Since I was at a loss how to investigate these matters, I asked whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges.
But when Paul appealed to be held for the Emperor’s decision, I ordered him to be held until I could send him up to Caesar.”

verse.note: The Greek word is the equivalent of the Latin title “Augustus,” borne by every Roman emperor after the first. Older versions print “Augustus,” which a modern reader is likely to take as the name of the first emperor, who was long dead. The reigning emperor was Nero. The word differs from “Caesar” at the end of the verse, so the two are rendered differently.

verse.text: Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you will hear him.”

So the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pageantry and entered the audience hall along with the military tribunes and the most prominent men of the city. Then Festus gave the order, and Paul was brought in.

And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all you who are present with us, you see this man, about whom the whole community of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.

text.q: But I found that he had done nothing deserving death, and when he himself appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him.

But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. So I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination has been held I may have something to write.

verse.note: Festus refers to the emperor simply as “the lord.” This way of referring to the emperor was becoming common in the eastern provinces at about this time. It is lowercase here because it does not refer to God or to Jesus, though early Christian readers would have noticed the same title they gave to Jesus.

text.q: For it seems to me unreasonable to send a prisoner without also indicating the charges against him.”

verse.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:

text.q: “I consider myself blessed, King Agrippa, that it is before you I am about to make my defense today concerning everything I am accused of by Jews,
especially because you are well acquainted with all the customs and disputes among Jews. So I beg you to listen to me patiently.
Now, my way of life from my youth, lived from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known to all Jews.

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one rendered “Gentiles” in verses 17, 20 and 23. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Paul’s own; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. In those later verses it is set against “the people,” a standing term for Israel.

text.q: They have known me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest party of our religion.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “sect,” which most translations keep. In the period the word named a recognized school or party within a larger body, as it does for the Pharisees and Sadducees, without the modern suggestion of a breakaway fringe group. “Party” is used to avoid that suggestion.

text.q: And now I stand here on trial because of hope in the promise God made to our fathers,
a promise our twelve tribes hope to attain as they worship earnestly night and day. It is about this hope, O king, that I am accused by Jews!
Why is it judged unbelievable among you that God raises the dead?
I myself, indeed, was convinced that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is what I did in Jerusalem. I locked up many of the holy ones in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death I cast my vote against them.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing Septuagint language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

The Greek is literally “I cast down a pebble,” the ordinary idiom for voting, since pebbles were used as ballots. If meant literally, it implies Paul sat on a body that passed sentence, perhaps the council in Jerusalem. Many scholars take it as a figure of speech for his approval of the executions; the question is unsettled.

text.q: In all the synagogues I often punished them and tried to force them to blaspheme, and, utterly out of my mind with rage against them, I persecuted them even as far as foreign cities.

note.term: tried to force them to blaspheme

verse.note: The Greek tense can describe either a repeated action or an attempted one. Most modern translations take it as an attempt (“tried to force”), which leaves open whether Paul succeeded; older versions have “compelled,” implying that he did. To blaspheme here would mean to curse or renounce Jesus.

text.q: While doing this, I was traveling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,
when at midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language,
‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

verse.note: The phrase can mean Hebrew proper or Aramaic, the related everyday language of Jews in Judea and Galilee; Greek writers of the period did not always distinguish them. Many scholars and several translations take it as Aramaic here, but the matter is disputed. The name is given in its Semitic form, “Saoul,” not the Greek form used elsewhere in the narrative.

A goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen; an animal that kicked back at it only hurt itself. The expression was a well-known Greek proverb for futile resistance to a greater power, especially a divine one, and is found in classical writers such as Euripides.

text.q: And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said,
‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

But get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and witness both of the things in which you have seen me and of those in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you

verse.note: The verb usually means “rescue” or “deliver,” and most translations take it so here. It can also mean “choose out” or “select,” which would give “choosing you out from the people and from the Gentiles.” The first fits the verb’s other uses in Acts and the echo of God’s promise to rescue the prophet Jeremiah.

text.q: to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, and so receive forgiveness of sins and a share among those who have been made holy by faith in me.’

note.term: those who have been made holy

verse.note: Most mainstream translations use “sanctified.” The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word behind “holy ones” in verse 10, and “made holy” keeps that link visible. The closing phrase “by faith in me” may attach to being made holy or to receiving forgiveness and a share; the Greek word order allows either.

text.q: So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,

but I declared first to those in Damascus and in Jerusalem, and throughout the whole region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should turn back and turn to God, doing deeds worthy of that turning back.

verse.note: Most translations have “repent” and “repentance” here, as established terms understood to include a change of life. “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry, while the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. It stands here beside a second verb, “turn to God,” which names the goal of the turning.

text.q: Because of this, Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
So, having obtained help from God, I stand to this day testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said was going to happen:
that the Messiah was to suffer and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he was to proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “Christ.” Here the word is a title under discussion, the anointed king Israel expected, and not a name, so “Messiah” is used, as in several modern translations. The two clauses are introduced in Greek by “whether,” as though listing the points under debate: whether the Messiah is to suffer, and whether he is the first to rise.

verse.text: As he was making this defense, Festus said in a loud voice, “You are out of your mind, Paul! Your great learning is driving you out of your mind.”
But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am declaring words of truth and of a sound mind.

text.q: For the king knows about these things, and to him I am speaking freely. For I am not persuaded that any of this has escaped his notice, since this was not done in a corner.
Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”

verse.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “In so little time you are trying to persuade me to become a Christian?”

note.traditional: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian

verse.note: Agrippa’s reply is one of the most disputed sentences in Acts. The older rendering “almost” is now generally rejected; the phrase means “in a little,” either “in a short time” or “with so little argument.” The tone may be ironic or evasive rather than sincere, and the last words can also be read as “to play the Christian.” Paul’s answer picks up the same phrase: “whether in little or in much.”

verse.text: And Paul said, “Whether in little time or much, I would pray to God that not only you but also all who are listening to me today might become such as I am—apart from these chains.”
Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them,
and after withdrawing they talked with one another, saying, “This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
When it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.
verse.note: A cohort was a Roman army unit of several hundred men. “Augustan” was an honorary title given to some auxiliary units, and inscriptions attest a cohort with this title stationed in Syria in the first century. Whether that is the unit meant here cannot be proved.

verse.text: We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for.
Putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us,
and after sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us aboard it.
For a good many days we sailed slowly and arrived off Cnidus with difficulty. Since the wind would not let us go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete, off Salmone,
and coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
Since a good deal of time had passed and the voyage was by now dangerous, because even the Fast had already gone by, Paul gave his advice,
verse.note: “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or early October. Ancient sailors regarded the open Mediterranean as dangerous from about mid-September and closed to shipping from about mid-November until spring, so the voyage was already running into the risky season.

verse.text: saying to them, “Men, I can see that the voyage is going to bring damage and heavy loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and the shipowner rather than by what Paul said.

Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, in the hope of somehow reaching Phoenix and wintering there—a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest.

note.traditional: lieth toward the south west and north west

verse.note: The Greek says the harbor looks “along” the southwest wind and the northwest wind. This may mean it faces the quarters those winds blow from (southwest and northwest), or the directions toward which they blow (northeast and southeast). The choice affects which bay on the south coast of Crete is meant, and the identification remains disputed.

verse.text: When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had achieved their purpose; they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close inshore.
But before long a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts give the wind’s name as Eurakylon, a sailors’ compound of the Greek word for the east wind and the Latin word for the north wind, hence an east-northeast gale. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Euroclydon”. Most modern versions translate the name as here.

verse.text: The ship was caught up and could not face into the wind, so we gave way and were carried along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to get control of the ship’s boat.
After hoisting it aboard, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and so were carried along.
verse.note: The Syrtis was the name for the gulfs off the coast of Libya, whose shallows and shifting sandbanks were notorious among ancient sailors. A ship driven southwest from Crete by a northeast gale would be heading toward them.

The Greek word is a general term for equipment. The crew may have lowered the mainsail and its yard to reduce the ship’s speed, or let down a sea anchor to drag behind and slow the drift. The translation keeps the general word because the Greek does not specify.

verse.text: As we were being violently battered by the storm, the next day they began to jettison the cargo,
and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars had appeared for many days and no small storm kept pressing on us, all hope of our being saved was finally being taken away.
After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not put out to sea from Crete, and spared yourselves this damage and loss.

text.q: And now I advise you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood by me
and said,
‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar; and look, God has granted you all those who are sailing with you.’
So take heart, men, for I trust God that it will be just as I have been told.
But we must run aground on some island.”

verse.text: When the fourteenth night came, as we were drifting across the Sea of Adria, about midnight the sailors began to suspect that they were nearing land.
verse.note: In the first century this name covered not only the modern Adriatic but the central Mediterranean between Greece and Crete on one side and Italy and Sicily on the other. A ship drifting west from Crete toward Malta was therefore in “Adria”.

verse.text: They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little farther on they took another sounding and found fifteen fathoms.
Fearing that we might run aground somewhere on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.
When the sailors tried to escape from the ship and lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they were going to lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it fall away.
As day was about to break, Paul urged everyone to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting in suspense and going without food, taking nothing.

text.q: So I urge you to take some food; this is for your survival, for not a hair from the head of any of you will be lost.”

verse.text: After saying this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.

note.term: he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it

verse.note: The sequence of taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it echoes Luke’s accounts of Jesus feeding the crowds and of the Last Supper. Most interpreters understand this as the ordinary Jewish thanksgiving before a meal, since most of those present were not believers, though Luke probably intends the echo. Some see a celebration of the Lord’s Supper.

verse.text: Then they all took heart, and they too took some food.
In all we were two hundred seventy-six people on the ship.
verse.note: The Greek word, often rendered “soul”, is used here in the Septuagint manner to count individuals, as in the older English “two hundred souls on board”. “People” gives the plain sense; in verses 10 and 22 the same word is rendered “life”.

verse.text: When they had eaten their fill, they began lightening the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, and they planned to run the ship ashore on it if they could.
They cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time untying the ropes that held the steering oars. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach.
But they came upon a spot where two seas met and ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was being broken up by the violence.

note.term: a spot where two seas met
note.traditional: a place where two seas met

verse.note: The rare Greek adjective means literally “of two seas”. It may describe a sandbank or reef with water on both sides, which is why many modern versions have “sandbar” or “reef”, or a channel or point of land where two bodies of water meet. The translation keeps the literal sense because the exact feature is uncertain.

note.traditional: with the violence of the waves

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “the violence of the waves”. The earliest witnesses lack “of the waves”, and the Greek text translated here follows them; the pounding of the surf is in any case what is meant.

verse.text: The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim away and escape.
verse.note: Roman soldiers were held personally answerable for prisoners in their charge and could pay with their own lives if one escaped. Acts 12:19 and 16:27 show the same rule at work.

verse.text: But the centurion, wanting to bring Paul safely through, kept them from carrying out their intention. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land,
and the rest to follow, some on planks and others on pieces from the ship. And so it came about that all were brought safely through to land.

note.traditional: on broken pieces of the ship

verse.note: The Greek says literally “on some of the ones from the ship”, and the form could refer to things or to people. Most translators understand pieces of wreckage; a minority take it to mean that some who could not swim were carried by members of the crew.

verse.text: When we had come through safely, we then learned that the island was called Malta.
The natives showed us no ordinary kindness: they lit a fire and took us all in, because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold.
verse.note: The Greek word names people who did not speak Greek; the Maltese of this period spoke a Punic dialect. It carries no suggestion of savagery here, as the praise of their kindness shows, so “barbarians” would mislead. Most modern translations likewise use “natives” or “islanders.”

verse.text: When Paul had gathered a bundle of brushwood and put it on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “This man must certainly be a murderer. He came through the sea safely, but Justice has not allowed him to live.”
verse.note: The islanders speak of Justice as a divine power that pursues the guilty, a familiar figure in Greek thought, where she was personified as a goddess. Their reasoning is that a man who escapes shipwreck only to be bitten by a snake must be a criminal whom divine retribution has caught. The capital letter reflects this personification, which most modern translations also recognize.

verse.text: He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited expectantly for a long time and saw nothing unusual happening to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
In the neighborhood of that place there were estates belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days.

note.term: the leading man of the island
note.traditional: the chief man of the island

verse.note: The phrase is literally “the first man of the island.” It appears to be an official local title and not just a description of prominence; inscriptions from Malta are usually cited as attesting it. Whether Publius was the Roman governor’s representative or a native dignitary is not certain.

verse.text: It happened that Publius’s father was lying ill, suffering from bouts of fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After this happened, the rest of the people on the island who had illnesses also came and were cured.
They also honored us with many honors, and when we were putting out to sea they supplied us with what we needed.
