After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered at the island, an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Gods as its figurehead.
verse.note: The Greek names the Dioscuri, the twin sons of Zeus, Castor and Pollux, who were regarded as protectors of sailors. Ships commonly carried a carved or painted emblem of a patron deity at the bow, which also served as the ship’s name.

verse.text: Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed three days.
From there we cast off and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,

note.traditional: we fetched a compass, we made a circuit

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between a word meaning “taking away,” probably a nautical term for weighing anchor or casting off (compare its use with anchors in 27:40), and a similar-looking word meaning “going around,” that is, sailing a roundabout course. The SBLGNT prints the first, which is followed here, though its exact nautical sense is uncertain.

verse.text: where we found brothers and sisters and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers and sisters there, having heard about us, came out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.

note.term: the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns
note.traditional: Appii Forum and The Three Taverns

verse.note: These were stopping places on the Appian Way, roughly forty and thirty miles south of Rome. Two groups of believers thus traveled a day or more out from the city to escort Paul in, the kind of reception customarily given to an honored visitor.

verse.text: When we entered Rome, Paul was permitted to live by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.

note.term: Paul was permitted to live by himself

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add before this clause that the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the camp; the words appear in the King James Version. The earliest witnesses lack them, and the SBLGNT does not include them.

verse.text: Three days later he called together the leading men of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the ancestral customs, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
verse.note: This translation renders the verb “hand over” throughout, so that the reader can see the same word used of Jesus being handed over to the authorities and of Paul here. The phrasing echoes the prophecy of Agabus in 21:11 and the predictions of Jesus’s own suffering. Older versions have “delivered”; many modern ones already use “handed over” in this verse.

text.q: When they had examined me, they wanted to release me, because there was no ground for a death sentence in my case.
But when the Jews spoke against this, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any accusation to bring against my nation.

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one translated “Gentiles” in verse 28. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Israel; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. The translation follows the standard practice of dividing the two by sense.

text.q: For this reason, then, I have invited you here to see you and speak with you, for it is because of the hope of Israel that I wear this chain.”

verse.text: They said to him, “We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers come here and reported or said anything bad about you.

text.q: But we think it right to hear from you what your views are, for as to this sect, it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere.”

verse.text: They set a day with him and came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning until evening he explained and testified to the kingdom of God, trying to persuade them about Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were persuaded by what was said, but others would not believe.
Disagreeing with one another, they began to leave after Paul had said one thing: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your ancestors,

text.q: saying, ‘Go to this people and say, “You will hear and hear but never understand, and you will look and look but never see.

For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they have barely heard, and their eyes they have closed, so that they might never see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.”’
So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles. They will indeed hear.”

verse.note: The verse numbered 29 in older English Bibles (“And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not printed in the SBLGNT. It is generally regarded as a later addition, so the numbering passes from 28 to 30.

verse.text: He stayed two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him,
verse.note: The Greek noun ordinarily means a price paid or rent, which gives “at his own expense.” Many translations instead take it as “in his own rented lodging,” which suits the verb “stayed” but is a sense not clearly attested for the word elsewhere. Either way the practical picture is the same: Paul lived in private quarters that he paid for, not in a prison.

verse.text: proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, unhindered.
